AI.result: On CIFAR-10 over fading channels, semantic inference accuracy stays high under shared wireless access and performance improves significantly under severe data imbalance; simultaneous transmission reduces training overhead while preserving robust performance across heterogeneous datasets.
AI.conclusion: Combining FL with semantic communication supports scalable, communication-efficient edge intelligence in future wireless networks.

title: Meta-Initialization of Implicit Neural Representations to Accelerate Deformable Medical Image Registration
comment: 14 pages, 5 figures, 2 tables. English-language author version of a paper presented at GraphiCon 2026, Saint Petersburg, Russia, 22-24 September 2026. Russian-language proceedings forthcoming. Related work updated for this version
summary: Implicit neural representation (INR) methods for deformable medical image registration require the network parameters to be optimized for each new image pair, making adaptation speed a practical limitation. This work investigates whether early adaptation can be accelerated using an initialization learned from a collection of previously solved registration tasks. We examine two schemes: Reptile meta-initialization and STRAINER transfer of the shared component of a coordinate network. KAN-IDIR is used as the base INR displacement-field model. Experiments are conducted on OASIS-1, with 364 consecutive pairs used for training and 49 pairs for test-time adaptation. Registration quality is evaluated using mean Dice and HD95, together with the fraction of voxels with a negative Jacobian determinant at iteration 1500. In the configurations studied, both schemes yield higher Dice and lower HD95 at early iterations than random initialization. Reptile numerically outperforms STRAINER under a small iteration budget, although their pretraining budgets are not matched. As the number of iterations increases, the differences between the schemes shrink. STRAINER pretraining takes 39-40 minutes, compared with 44.98 hours for Reptile.

AI.tldr: Meta-initialization of implicit neural representations for deformable registration, using Reptile or transferred STRAINER weights, gives higher Dice and lower HD95 at early iterations than random initialization on OASIS-1. The advantage shrinks as the number of iterations grows.
AI.motivation: INR-based deformable registration optimizes network parameters for every new image pair, so adaptation speed is a practical limitation.
AI.method: Two initialization schemes, Reptile meta-initialization and STRAINER transfer of the shared component of a coordinate network, applied to the KAN-IDIR displacement-field INR; 364 consecutive OASIS-1 pairs are used for training and 49 pairs for test-time adaptation.
AI.result: Both schemes give higher Dice and lower HD95 at early iterations than random initialization; Reptile numerically outperforms STRAINER under a small iteration budget although pretraining budgets are not matched; STRAINER pretraining takes 39-40 minutes versus 44.98 hours for Reptile; the differences shrink as iterations increase.
AI.conclusion: Learned initialization can accelerate early adaptation of INR registration, with STRAINER far cheaper to pretrain than Reptile, while the benefit of either diminishes with more iterations.

title: FORGE: Feasible Online Reduced-Order Reference Generation and Whole-Body Execution for Agile Humanoid Locomotion
comment: 8 pages, 6 figures. Accepted to the 2026 IEEE-RAS 25th International Conference on Humanoid Robots (Humanoids)
summary: This paper presents a two-stage learning framework for versatile and agile humanoid locomotion that couples online reduced-order model (ROM) reference generation with whole-body tracking control. In the first stage, we train a command-conditioned whole-body reference generator using single rigid body dynamics combined with full humanoid kinematics. In the second stage, the frozen ROM policy is rolled out online to generate references for training a whole-body tracking policy on the full-order dynamics model. Learning a kino-dynamically consistent reference generator in the simplified ROM space enables us to generate references over a broad command space and over multiple locomotion strategies using a single unified framework. We demonstrate the approach on a Unitree G1 humanoid robot, achieving longitudinal velocities from -2.0 m/s to 2.8 m/s, lateral velocities up to +-1.0 m/s, angular velocities up to +-3.0 rad/s, one-legged hopping, and continuous transitions across the commands, all using one unified reference policy and one whole-body tracking policy.

AI.tldr: FORGE is a two-stage framework for agile humanoid locomotion that trains a reduced-order-model reference generator and then a whole-body tracking policy. On a Unitree G1 robot it achieves longitudinal velocities from -2.0 to 2.8 m/s, lateral velocities up to +-1.0 m/s, angular velocities up to +-3.0 rad/s and one-legged hopping, using one reference policy and one tracking policy.
AI.motivation: Versatile and agile humanoid locomotion requires whole-body references that are kinodynamically consistent over a broad command space and multiple locomotion strategies.
AI.method: In the first stage, a command-conditioned whole-body reference generator is trained with single rigid body dynamics combined with full humanoid kinematics; in the second stage, the frozen ROM policy is rolled out online to generate references for training a whole-body tracking policy on the full-order dynamics model.
AI.result: On a Unitree G1 humanoid the approach reaches longitudinal velocities from -2.0 to 2.8 m/s, lateral velocities up to +-1.0 m/s, angular velocities up to +-3.0 rad/s, one-legged hopping and continuous transitions across commands, all with one unified reference policy and one whole-body tracking policy.
AI.conclusion: Learning kinodynamically consistent references in a simplified reduced-order space yields a single unified framework that covers a broad command space and multiple locomotion strategies.

title: New Multiple Descent Phenomena Induced by Heterogeneous Data
summary: Modern machine learning models are often trained on large datasets assembled from many different sources, whose statistical properties can differ substantially. Understanding how this heterogeneity affects generalization performance is therefore important for explaining how model performance changes as model size increases. In this work, we study this question in linear random-feature models and show that mixtures of datasets with different covariance structures can give rise to a range of multiple-descent phenomena. We derive exact asymptotic expressions for the test error of each data source in the high-dimensional regime, and show how heterogeneity in covariance scale and spectral structure can introduce additional, group-dependent interpolation thresholds as model size increases. These phenomena arise even with noiseless labels and linear activations, showing that neither label noise nor activation nonlinearity is necessary for multiple-descent. Our results therefore provide a different perspective from classical explanations of multiple descent. More broadly, our results have potential implications for algorithmic fairness by showing that model scaling can affect different data groups unevenly, amplifying disparities in their generalization errors. We validate our theoretical results on synthetic Gaussian mixtures and real-world datasets, including MNIST and CIFAR-10.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that mixtures of datasets with different covariance structures in linear random-feature models produce multiple-descent curves even with noiseless labels and linear activations. It derives exact asymptotic test errors per data source and notes implications for fairness across groups.
AI.motivation: Modern models are trained on heterogeneous datasets whose statistics differ, and classical explanations of multiple descent rely on label noise or activation nonlinearity.
AI.method: Analysis of linear random-feature models trained on mixtures of datasets with different covariance structures; exact asymptotic expressions for the test error of each data source in the high-dimensional regime; validation on synthetic Gaussian mixtures and on MNIST and CIFAR-10.
AI.result: Heterogeneity in covariance scale and spectral structure introduces additional, group-dependent interpolation thresholds as model size increases, giving multiple descent without label noise or activation nonlinearity.
AI.conclusion: Model scaling can affect different data groups unevenly, potentially amplifying disparities in generalization error, which offers a different perspective from classical multiple-descent explanations.

title: Finite-step statistical mechanics of scale-invariant learning: spectral equations of state and curvature transport
summary: Stationary learning admits an ideal-gas description under restrictive noise assumptions. In neural networks whose gradient noise departs from these assumptions, however, an entropy-scaling relation resembling a Maxwell relation remains approximately valid. We ask which thermodynamic-looking relations follow from scale symmetry rather than equilibrium, and how departures from the ideal-gas description can be quantified, for discrete stochastic gradient dynamics with memory. An exact rescaling of trajectories explains the entropy relation without assuming thermal equilibrium. Within a local harmonic approximation, self-adjusting weight norms yield a spectral equation of state whose virial coefficients are set by moments of the curvature spectrum, and coupled parameter groups can sustain stationary probability currents. Our central result beyond this approximation is an exact curvature-transport identity. Together with a finite-step loss balance, it decomposes corrections to the harmonic fluctuation relation into measurable curvature changes, finite-step remainders, gradient-memory correlations and finite-window drift terms. A related displacement-weighted curvature change provides a diagnostic of the arrow of time; its mean and second moment give a lower bound on the relative entropy between forward and reversed state pairs. We also calculate the activation-boundary contribution to curvature for rectified teacher-student networks with Gaussian inputs. Tests in sphere models, teacher-student networks and convolutional networks on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 support the transport description and identify limits of the harmonic and cubic-remainder approximations. These results separate symmetry-based relations from equilibrium assumptions and provide quantitative diagnostics of nonideal fluctuations in learning dynamics.

AI.tldr: The paper derives exact relations for discrete stochastic gradient dynamics with memory from scale symmetry rather than equilibrium, including a curvature-transport identity that decomposes corrections to the harmonic fluctuation relation. Experiments on sphere models, teacher-student networks and CNNs on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 support the description.
AI.motivation: Stationary learning has an ideal-gas description only under restrictive noise assumptions, and the paper asks which thermodynamic-like relations follow from scale symmetry and how departures from the ideal-gas description can be quantified.
AI.method: An exact rescaling of trajectories explains the entropy relation without assuming thermal equilibrium; under a local harmonic approximation, self-adjusting weight norms give a spectral equation of state whose virial coefficients are set by moments of the curvature spectrum; an exact curvature-transport identity, together with a finite-step loss balance, decomposes the corrections; a displacement-weighted curvature change serves as an arrow-of-time diagnostic.
AI.result: The displacement-weighted curvature change has a mean and second moment that give a lower bound on the relative entropy between forward and reversed state pairs; experiments on sphere models, teacher-student networks and CNNs on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 support the transport description and identify limits of the harmonic and cubic-remainder approximations.
AI.conclusion: The results separate symmetry-based relations from equilibrium assumptions and provide quantitative diagnostics of nonideal fluctuations in learning dynamics.

title: Efficient Deep Gaussian Process Surrogates via Mini-Batch Latent MAP Estimation
comment: 35 pages including references, 11 pages appendix, 5 figures
summary: Deep Gaussian processes (DGPs) are flexible surrogate models for computer experiments with nonstationary response surfaces, but inference over their latent representations remains computationally challenging. Existing methods typically rely on variational inference or Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC), which impose variational-family assumptions or require costly posterior sampling. We propose the latent maximum-a-posteriori deep Gaussian process (LaMP-DGP), which uses gradient-based optimization to obtain MAP estimates of the latent representations and enables efficient probabilistic prediction through linked-GP calculations. To scale LaMP-DGP to large datasets, we develop a mini-batch optimization algorithm and, under a polynomial mini-batch bias-decay condition, establish a stationarity bound for latent-state optimization that motivates a growing batch-size schedule. Across numerical experiments and real-data analyses, LaMP-DGP provides consistently competitive predictive performance relative to doubly stochastic variational inference, stochastic gradient Hamiltonian Monte Carlo, and fully Bayesian Vecchia DGP inference. Computationally, LaMP-DGP is substantially faster than the Vecchia MCMC approach while remaining broadly competitive with the stochastic-gradient alternatives. These results position LaMP-DGP as a competitive and computationally efficient alternative for DGP inference. An R package, "LaMPDGP", is available for implementing the proposed method.

AI.tldr: LaMP-DGP obtains MAP estimates of latent representations in deep Gaussian process surrogates with gradient-based optimization and a mini-batch algorithm for large datasets. It is competitive with doubly stochastic variational inference, stochastic gradient HMC and fully Bayesian Vecchia DGP inference, and is substantially faster than the Vecchia MCMC approach.
AI.motivation: Existing DGP inference relies on variational inference, which imposes variational-family assumptions, or on MCMC, which requires costly posterior sampling.
AI.method: Gradient-based MAP estimation of latent representations with probabilistic prediction through linked-GP calculations; a mini-batch optimization algorithm with a growing batch-size schedule, motivated by a stationarity bound under a polynomial mini-batch bias-decay condition.
AI.result: Across numerical experiments and real-data analyses, LaMP-DGP gives consistently competitive predictive performance relative to the stochastic-gradient and fully Bayesian baselines, and is substantially faster than the Vecchia MCMC approach while remaining broadly competitive with the stochastic-gradient alternatives.
AI.conclusion: LaMP-DGP is a competitive and computationally efficient alternative for DGP inference, with an R package, LaMPDGP, available for implementation.

title: Conformal Predictive Distributions for Contextual Order Fulfillment Optimization
summary: Ship-to-home fulfillment requires a retailer to select a fulfillment location and carrier before the delivery time is known. These decisions often rely on static transit-time estimates, which cannot represent how delivery-time uncertainty varies across orders and fulfillment options. This paper constructs conformal predictive distributions (CPDs) using Conformal Predictive Systems (CPS) for regression and the cross Venn-Abers predictor (CVAP) for multiclass classification, and uses them in a contextual optimization model for fulfillment decisions. The model is solved by contextual sample-average approximation (C-SAA). The regret of each fulfillment decision, its expected cost above that of the best decision, is bounded by forecast error, scenario-evaluation error, and the candidate-generation gap. The forecast term depends on how well calibration residuals or class probabilities represent the current order. On more than five million proprietary order records, CVAP raises exact-day accuracy from 49.5% for the rule-based estimate to 64.1%. Paired with a decision rule that selects a quantile weighting late errors more heavily, the split CPS (SCPS) gives a point estimate that raises late-delivery detection from 3.8% to 79.4%. Residual-based CPS distributions also meet or slightly exceed nominal interval-coverage targets. In decision experiments with a this http URL simulator over six test dates, C-SAA with CVAP lowers mean total cost by 7.1% and C-SAA with the Mondrian CPS (MCPS) lowers it by 6.7%, relative to C-SAA with the original nonconformal forecast. Both cut the late-delivery rate from 5.7% to below 4.0%.

AI.tldr: The paper builds conformal predictive distributions for delivery-time uncertainty and uses them in contextual sample-average optimization of ship-to-home fulfillment decisions. On over five million proprietary order records and in simulation, the calibrated models improve prediction and lower mean total cost by 6.7% to 7.1%.
AI.motivation: Fulfillment decisions rely on static transit-time estimates that cannot represent how delivery-time uncertainty varies across orders and fulfillment options.
AI.method: Conformal Predictive Systems for regression and the cross Venn-Abers predictor for multiclass classification construct conformal predictive distributions, which feed a contextual sample-average approximation (C-SAA) decision model; a split CPS with a quantile that weights late errors more heavily gives a point estimate; regret is bounded by forecast error, scenario-evaluation error and the candidate-generation gap.
AI.result: On over five million proprietary order records, CVAP raises exact-day accuracy from 49.5% to 64.1%, and split CPS raises late-delivery detection from 3.8% to 79.4%; in simulation over six test dates, C-SAA with CVAP lowers mean total cost by 7.1% and C-SAA with Mondrian CPS by 6.7%, both cutting the late-delivery rate from 5.7% to below 4.0%.
AI.conclusion: Calibrated conformal predictive distributions improve fulfillment decisions by making delivery-time uncertainty explicit within the optimization.

title: Cooperative EV Charging Assignment Using Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning: A Comparison of QMIX and Independent Q-Learning Under Urban Traffic Uncertainty
comment: 14 pages, 7 figures. Presented at ICATH 2026 (Rabat, Morocco, 15-17 July 2026); accepted for publication in MDPI Engineering Proceedings (in press)
summary: The allocation of electric vehicles to public charging stations is increasingly constrained by the fact that several heterogeneous facilities often serve the same stream of requests while observing only partial local information. An accept/reject decision that is defensible for one station may nevertheless reduce the efficiency of the charging district as a whole. We formulate this operational problem as a Decentralized Partially Observable Markov Decision Process (Dec-POMDP) and examine whether Centralized Training with Decentralized Execution (CTDE), instantiated through QMIX, improves assignment performance relative to a cooperative Independent Q-Learning baseline (IQL). The evaluation uses a six-station urban network simulated with SUMO, five independent random seeds, 200 training episodes, and four traffic flux scenarios ranging from 100 to 250 vehicles/hour. Under this protocol, QMIX reaches a mean reward per evaluated decision of +0.776, versus +0.578 for IQL (delta = +0.198, seed-paired Cohens dz = 2.98, exact two-sided Wilcoxon p = 0.0625, the minimum attainable value at this sample size), and raises the acceptance rate from 72.4% to 94.0% (delta = +21.6 pp, dz = 5.24, Wilcoxon p = 0.0625). A five-variant ablation suggests this gain is primarily attributable to the CTDE architecture when holding cooperative reward terms fixed, though not formally isolated with a single seed. By contrast, cooperative reward shaping and experience sharing show no clear descriptive benefit and may slightly reduce performance. These findings support the view that, for multi-station charging assignment, coordination should be embedded in the learning architecture rather than added only through heuristic cooperation terms.

AI.tldr: QMIX, a centralized-training decentralized-execution method, outperforms independent Q-learning for assigning electric vehicles to six charging stations in a SUMO urban simulation, raising mean reward from 0.578 to 0.776 and acceptance from 72.4% to 94.0%. An ablation suggests the gain comes mainly from the architecture rather than from cooperative reward shaping or experience sharing.
AI.motivation: Several heterogeneous stations serve the same stream of requests while observing only partial local information, so a locally defensible accept or reject decision can reduce the efficiency of the whole district.
AI.method: The problem is formulated as a Dec-POMDP; QMIX is compared with a cooperative Independent Q-Learning baseline on a six-station network simulated in SUMO, with five seeds, 200 training episodes and four traffic flux scenarios from 100 to 250 vehicles per hour; a five-variant ablation tests the cooperative reward terms and experience sharing.
AI.result: QMIX reaches a mean reward per evaluated decision of +0.776 versus +0.578 for IQL (delta +0.198, seed-paired Cohen's dz 2.98, exact two-sided Wilcoxon p = 0.0625, the minimum attainable at this sample size) and raises acceptance from 72.4% to 94.0%; cooperative reward shaping and experience sharing show no clear benefit and may slightly reduce performance.
AI.conclusion: For multi-station charging assignment, coordination should be embedded in the learning architecture rather than added only through heuristic cooperation terms, although the single-seed ablation does not formally isolate this effect.

title: Progressive-Observation Physical-Layer Fingerprinting for Efficient Open-Set Ethernet Authentication
comment: 6 pages, 5 figures, 2 tables. Submitted to IEEE ICC 2027
summary: Physical-layer fingerprinting (PLF) has emerged as a promising authentication approach for Internet of Things devices. However, most PLF systems acquire and process a fixed-length waveform for every authentication query, burdening resource-constrained edge nodes. To address this issue, we propose a progressive-observation PLF method that adapts the waveform length to each query. Specifically, a lightweight convolutional neural network (CNN) first rejects clearly unknown devices from a short observation. Spectral matching then accepts clearly registered devices from a slightly longer observation. Only ambiguous queries proceed to the same matching on the full-length waveform, reducing both data acquisition and computation. Because fingerprints drift across days, we also design an adaptive calibration algorithm to avoid retraining the CNN. The algorithm realigns the features and decision thresholds using a few current-day references from registered devices. We evaluate the method with 100BASE-TX Ethernet devices of two controller types on held-out days. Compared with fixed-length processing, it keeps the false rejection and false acceptance rates equal or lower for both controller types on both days. It also reduces the waveform data per query by 75.1% and the CPU processing time on a Raspberry Pi 5 by 73.7% on average. With the same monitoring bandwidth, an edge node can therefore serve about four times as many authentication queries.

AI.tldr: A progressive-observation physical-layer fingerprinting method adapts the waveform length to each authentication query, rejecting unknown devices from short observations and accepting registered devices from slightly longer ones. It keeps false rejection and false acceptance rates equal or lower than fixed-length processing while cutting waveform data per query by 75.1% and CPU time on a Raspberry Pi 5 by 73.7%.
AI.motivation: Most PLF systems acquire and process a fixed-length waveform for every query, which burdens resource-constrained edge nodes, and fingerprints drift across days.
AI.method: A lightweight CNN first rejects clearly unknown devices from a short observation; spectral matching accepts clearly registered devices from a slightly longer one; only ambiguous queries are processed on the full-length waveform; an adaptive calibration realigns features and decision thresholds using a few current-day references from registered devices, avoiding CNN retraining.
AI.result: Evaluated on 100BASE-TX Ethernet devices with two controller types on held-out days, the method keeps false rejection and false acceptance rates equal or lower than fixed-length processing for both controllers on both days, reduces waveform data per query by 75.1% and Raspberry Pi 5 CPU time by 73.7% on average, and lets an edge node serve about four times as many authentication queries at the same monitoring bandwidth.
AI.conclusion: Progressive observation combined with lightweight calibration makes open-set PLF authentication far more efficient on edge nodes without sacrificing error rates.

title: Neural Compression of Long ADMM Trajectory for Multiparametric Quadratic Program
comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026. Code: this https URL
summary: Solving large-scale multiparametric quadratic programs (mpQPs) in real time often requires thousands of iterative optimization updates, creating a major computational bottleneck in model predictive control and learning-enabled systems. This paper proposes TQPNet, a self-supervised neural compression framework that learns to compress long ADMM optimization trajectories into a compact neural warm start followed by a few refinement iterations. We derive a low-dimensional ADMM scheme operating on the primal-dual variables $(x,\beta)$ and show that its iteration admits an equivalent ReLU-layer representation, termed ADMM(ReLU). Building on this insight, TQPNet combines a multilayer perceptron with ReLU activations (MLP(ReLU)) and a small number of unrolled ADMM(ReLU) refinement layers. The network is trained offline using an optimality-condition-informed residual loss, eliminating the need for solver-generated labels. The proposed residual-based framework enables both self-supervised training and online solution certification through adaptive ADMM(ReLU) refinement. Experiments on large-scale mpQPs and real-time MPC applications demonstrate that TQPNet achieves high accuracy, strong generalization, and substantially faster inference than conventional optimization-based methods.

AI.tldr: TQPNet is a self-supervised neural compression framework that compresses long ADMM trajectories for multiparametric quadratic programs into a neural warm start followed by a few unrolled refinement iterations. It achieves high accuracy and substantially faster inference than conventional optimization methods on large-scale mpQPs and real-time MPC.
AI.motivation: Solving large-scale mpQPs in real time requires thousands of iterative updates, which is a major computational bottleneck in model predictive control and learning-enabled systems.
AI.method: A low-dimensional ADMM scheme on the primal-dual variables (x, beta) is shown to admit an equivalent ReLU-layer representation, ADMM(ReLU); TQPNet combines an MLP with ReLU activations and a few unrolled ADMM(ReLU) refinement layers, trained offline with an optimality-condition-informed residual loss and no solver-generated labels.
AI.result: Experiments on large-scale mpQPs and real-time MPC applications show high accuracy, strong generalization and substantially faster inference than conventional optimization-based methods.
AI.conclusion: The residual-based framework enables both self-supervised training and online solution certification through adaptive ADMM(ReLU) refinement.

title: Interpretable Feature Discovery from Unstructured Data Using LLMs and Statistical Choice Models
comment: Preprint. 88 pages, 21 figures, 12 tables. Code: this https URL
summary: Feature extraction from unstructured data typically relies on opaque embeddings unsuited to interpretable decision-making. Interpretable features, on the other hand, typically require costly, and often infeasible, hand-engineering. Large language models (LLMs) offer a natural bridge, as they can read raw data and describe it in interpretable terms. One could simply ask an LLM to extract features from a large sample of the dataset, but context limitations and diluted attention can lead to unsatisfactory results. We introduce a method that automatically discovers interpretable, decision-relevant features from unstructured data. Our key idea is to perform pairwise comparisons between items, asking an LLM to articulate, in interpretable terms, the features distinguishing each pair. We treat these explanations, or rationales, as data: we develop a statistical choice model that combines these rationales across the comparisons to identify relevant features and estimate per-item, per-feature scores. We first test our method on a synthetic hiring dataset of cover letters with known ground-truth features and show that it significantly outperforms direct LLM feature extraction in feature recovery. We then apply it to the ChangeMyView (Reddit) debate dataset, where it discovers several interpretable features associated with persuasion while reaching predictive accuracy comparable to established baselines. We also show how the same rationales can be used to audit LLM decisions, yielding a holistic score whose decomposition over interpretable features reveals what the LLM rewards.

AI.tldr: The method discovers interpretable, decision-relevant features from unstructured data by asking an LLM to explain pairwise differences between items and combining these rationales in a statistical choice model. It recovers ground-truth features on a synthetic hiring dataset, finds persuasion-related features on ChangeMyView, and can audit LLM decisions.
AI.motivation: Embeddings are opaque, hand-engineering interpretable features is costly, and asking an LLM to extract features directly from a large sample is limited by context length and diluted attention.
AI.method: Pairwise comparisons between items, with the LLM articulating the features that distinguish each pair; these rationales are treated as data and combined by a statistical choice model that identifies relevant features and estimates per-item, per-feature scores.
AI.result: On a synthetic hiring dataset of cover letters with known ground-truth features, the method significantly outperforms direct LLM feature extraction in feature recovery; on the ChangeMyView debate dataset it finds interpretable features associated with persuasion with predictive accuracy comparable to established baselines; the same rationales yield a holistic score whose decomposition reveals what the LLM rewards.
AI.conclusion: Pairwise LLM rationales modeled statistically offer a practical bridge from raw unstructured data to interpretable features and a way to audit LLM decisions.

title: Nemotron 3.5 Super and Lightning: Open, Efficient Mixture-of-Experts Hybrid Mamba-Transformer Models for Agentic AI
summary: We introduce Nemotron 3.5 Super and Nemotron 3.5 Lightning, open and efficient Mixture-of-Experts Hybrid Mamba-Transformer models designed for reasoning, long-context understanding, and agentic workloads. Super is a 120B-parameter, 12B-active multimodal model, while Lightning is a smaller 30B-parameter, 3B-active text model; both designed for efficient deployment. Both models combine large-scale distillation, long-context training, and native speculative decoding, while Super further incorporates Indic continued pretraining and agentic software-engineering mid-training. We develop a comprehensive post-training pipeline spanning supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning (RLVR and RLHF), complemented in Super by specialized teacher training and multi- teacher on-policy distillation (MOPD). This transforms Super from a text-only base model into a multimodal agent capable of reasoning over text, images, video, and interactive tool environments. We further explore test-time scaling through parallel agent execution and self-verification. Across training and deployment, we jointly optimize capability and efficiency. Indic continued pretraining improves Indian-language benchmarks by up to 9.82 percentage points, while agentic mid-training strengthens software-engineering capabilities and robustness across agent harnesses. The post-trained Super model achieves 51.78% on SWE-bench Pro, surpassing Nemotron 3 Ultra despite using approximately 4.6x fewer active parameters. Post-training MTP boosting improves speculative- decoding acceptance length by up to 21.8% under probabilistic draft sampling, while NVFP4 quantization achieves 99.62% median accuracy recovery relative to BF16. Inference optimizations enable up to 4,856 output tokens/s/GPU on GB200 while sustaining at least 50 tokens/s/user.

AI.tldr: Nemotron 3.5 Super (120B total, 12B active, multimodal) and Nemotron 3.5 Lightning (30B total, 3B active, text) are open MoE hybrid Mamba-Transformer models for reasoning and agentic workloads. Super reaches 51.78% on SWE-bench Pro, and NVFP4 quantization recovers 99.62% median accuracy relative to BF16.
AI.motivation: The paper aims to provide open, efficient models for reasoning, long-context understanding and agentic workloads that are cheap to deploy, jointly optimizing capability and efficiency.
AI.method: Large-scale distillation, long-context training and native speculative decoding for both models; Super additionally receives Indic continued pretraining and agentic software-engineering mid-training, a post-training pipeline of SFT and RL (RLVR and RLHF), specialized teacher training with multi-teacher on-policy distillation (MOPD), and test-time scaling through parallel agent execution and self-verification.
AI.result: Indic continued pretraining improves Indian-language benchmarks by up to 9.82 percentage points; post-trained Super reaches 51.78% on SWE-bench Pro, surpassing Nemotron 3 Ultra with about 4.6x fewer active parameters; post-training MTP boosting raises speculative-decoding acceptance length by up to 21.8%; NVFP4 quantization achieves 99.62% median accuracy recovery relative to BF16; inference reaches up to 4,856 output tokens/s/GPU on GB200 while sustaining at least 50 tokens/s/user.
AI.conclusion: Open MoE hybrid models can be post-trained into multimodal agents and deployed efficiently, with capability and efficiency optimized together.

title: Evaluating Causal Reasoning in LLMs: A Case Study in the Challenges of Procedural Generation
summary: Large language models (LLMs) appear to represent and reason about a large range of phenomena. In particular, recent studies have examined whether LLMs can accurately reason about causation. One of the most commonly used benchmarks for evaluating formal causal reasoning in LLMs is CLadder, a framework for procedural generation of benchmark data sets that was released in 2023. Experiments with CLadder appear to indicate that LLMs can perform formal causal reasoning in a large percentage of generated examples. In this paper, we examine what can be reliably inferred when LLMs perform well on test sets produced by CLadder. We identify several examples of superficial and highly predictive patterns that the CLadder generator embeds in data sets it generates. We find that even simple models such as random forests perform well on CLadder-generated data sets after training on a sample of generated data. We also find that the performance of many commercial LLMs on CLadder test sets is extremely brittle and that removing large sections of the text that are critical for formal causal reasoning has almost no effect on performance. Given these results, the most likely hypothesis for the strong performance of state-of-the-art LLMs on CLadder is that they are exploiting superficial patterns learned from exposure to training data from the generator. Any inference that LLMs are exhibiting more complex causal reasoning must rule out this hypothesis.

AI.tldr: Strong LLM performance on the CLadder causal reasoning benchmark is largely explained by superficial patterns the dataset generator embeds, since simple random forests also perform well and removing critical reasoning text barely changes results. The paper argues that any claim of complex causal reasoning must first rule out this explanation.
AI.motivation: CLadder is one of the most commonly used benchmarks for formal causal reasoning in LLMs, and reported results appear to show LLMs performing formal causal reasoning, but what those results establish is unclear.
AI.method: Identification of superficial, highly predictive patterns embedded by the CLadder generator; training random forests on a sample of generated data and testing them on CLadder test sets; evaluation of commercial LLMs on CLadder test sets after removing large sections of text critical for formal causal reasoning.
AI.result: Random forests perform well on CLadder-generated data after training on a sample of generated data; many commercial LLMs are extremely brittle on CLadder test sets, and removing critical reasoning text has almost no effect on their performance.
AI.conclusion: The most likely explanation for strong LLM performance on CLadder is exploitation of superficial generator patterns, so claims of complex causal reasoning must rule out this hypothesis first.

title: Same Label, Different Interface: Beyond Action-Space Labels in Robot Learning
summary: Robot-learning studies often compare position and velocity actions as though each label identified a single experimental treatment, yet the label alone does not determine what the robot executes. Before affecting robot motion, bounded policy output passes through filtering, physical scaling, reference construction, feedback, timing, and effort limits. We study how these omitted properties affect attribution under one shared learner and training budget. Across three contact-rich Factory tasks (PegInsert, GearMesh, and NutThread), we compare five joint-space interfaces, with ten independently trained policies per condition. We first remain within the same position-feedback law and vary the executed interface: substituting only the physical action scale as the directly modified component changes sample-median evaluation success by 0.645-1.000 across tasks, while removing an exponential moving average produces task-dependent changes. We then move to a cross-law comparison and choose a velocity scale that exactly matches the position interface's local raw-torque command gain. This calibration raises the sample median on GearMesh and NutThread, with no median change on PegInsert. Yet clear residual sample-median gaps remain on PegInsert and GearMesh, while the NutThread interval includes zero. Thus, even this explicit equality leaves feedback and held-action dynamics unmatched and does not establish position-velocity trained-outcome equivalence. Action-interface comparisons should therefore report the executed pathway and state the physical quantity they match.

AI.tldr: In contact-rich Factory robot tasks, the label position or velocity does not by itself determine what the robot executes, and matching a velocity interface to a position interface's raw-torque gain still leaves trained outcomes unmatched. The paper recommends reporting the executed pathway and the physical quantity each interface is matched on.
AI.motivation: Robot-learning studies compare position and velocity actions as if each label identified a single experimental treatment, but omitted properties such as filtering, physical scaling, feedback, timing and effort limits affect what is executed.
AI.method: Under one shared learner and training budget, five joint-space interfaces are compared on three Factory tasks (PegInsert, GearMesh, NutThread) with ten independently trained policies per condition; the physical action scale and an exponential moving average are varied within the position-feedback law, and a velocity scale is calibrated to match the position interface's local raw-torque command gain.
AI.result: Changing only the physical action scale changes sample-median evaluation success by 0.645 to 1.000 across tasks, and removing an exponential moving average produces task-dependent changes; the calibration raises the sample median on GearMesh and NutThread with no median change on PegInsert, while residual sample-median gaps remain on PegInsert and GearMesh and the NutThread interval includes zero.
AI.conclusion: Exact matching of the commanded gain does not establish position-velocity trained-outcome equivalence, so action-interface comparisons should report the executed pathway and state the physical quantity they match.

title: Who Called? V33DA: A Physically Verified Multimodal Benchmark for Vocal Attribution in Zebra Finch Groups
comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026 (Evaluations and Datasets Track). 43 pages, 3 figures. Dataset: this https URL ; Code: this https URL
summary: Deciding which member of an animal group produced a vocalization and where that vocalization was produced are central to studying social communication but are rarely evaluated with physically verified ground truth. Existing resources either localize sounds without identifying the caller, or recognize individuals from isolated vocalizations without reliance on the 3D candidate geometry. We close this gap with V33DA, a dataset-centered multimodal benchmark for spatial vocal attribution in social zebra finches: it comprises 33,625 verified events coupling 5-channel audio with three camera views, calibrated 3D pose for every visible candidate, and per-bird radio telemetry across 10 individuals and three experiments. Caller identity is verified from an on-body accelerometer-derived vibration signal; this channel is withheld from benchmark models and used only by an on-body reference ceiling. Given a detected vocalization and the visible candidate birds, the task is to select the caller. We evaluate it under three regimes: session-disjoint testing on familiar birds from held-out recording dates, held-out-experiment transfer to a new cohort, and leave-one-individual-out evaluation on a bird whose vocalizations are held out from training. Reference methods expose a consistent gap between in-domain accuracy and transfer to unseen individuals: methods that can exploit familiar vocal identity perform well on known callers but degrade sharply on unseen ones, whereas candidate-aware methods preserving explicit spatial reasoning transfer substantially better. The on-body reference stays near-perfect across regimes, confirming the internal consistency of the accelerometer-verified labels. We release V33DA with fixed protocols and code for the evaluated methods, and V33DA++, an unevaluated companion set of verified overlapping-call events and +/-2 s context windows.

AI.tldr: V33DA is a multimodal benchmark of 33,625 physically verified events for identifying which zebra finch in a group produced a vocalization, using 5-channel audio, three camera views, calibrated 3D pose and radio telemetry. Methods that exploit familiar vocal identity fail on unseen birds, while candidate-aware spatial methods transfer better.
AI.motivation: Existing resources either localize sounds without identifying the caller or recognize individuals from isolated vocalizations without 3D candidate geometry, and rarely provide physically verified ground truth.
AI.method: Caller identity is verified from an on-body accelerometer-derived vibration signal, which is withheld from benchmark models and used only for an on-body reference ceiling; the task is to select the caller among visible candidates given a detected vocalization, evaluated under session-disjoint testing, held-out-experiment transfer and leave-one-individual-out regimes.
AI.result: Reference methods show a consistent gap between in-domain accuracy and transfer to unseen individuals; methods that exploit familiar vocal identity perform well on known callers but degrade sharply on unseen ones, whereas candidate-aware methods that keep explicit spatial reasoning transfer substantially better; the on-body reference stays near-perfect across regimes.
AI.conclusion: The release of V33DA with fixed protocols, evaluated code and an unevaluated companion set, V33DA++, supports research on spatial vocal attribution in social animal groups.

title: Post-Training Large Language Models with LLMON
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) treat all context tokens uniformly, lacking explicit separation between executable instructions and passive data. This leads to prompt injection vulnerabilities, ambiguous instruction binding, and unreliable execution control. We present a post-training methodology using LLMON (LLM Object Notation), a framework that enables separating instructions from data and requires explicit identifier-based execution. We construct a large-scale structured training corpus of 4.6B tokens spanning general, RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation), and tool-calling data, augmented with distractor-infused variants in which competing instructions and irrelevant data segments are present in context but not referenced. Post-training two Granite-4.1 base models (3B and 8B) through supervised fine-tuning followed by reinforcement learning, we show that LLMON-structured supervision reduces attack success rates on indirect prompt-injection benchmarks from 53-100% to 0.02-5.6% while preserving general capabilities. We further introduce attention-based interpretability metrics that diagnose failure modes at individual transformer layers for structured inputs, revealing how our approach reshapes internal attention patterns. Our results demonstrate that explicit execution semantics can be taught through standard post-training without architectural modification.

AI.tldr: Post-training Granite-4.1 3B and 8B models with LLMON, an identifier-based notation that separates instructions from data, cuts attack success on indirect prompt-injection benchmarks from 53-100% to 0.02-5.6% while preserving general capabilities. The method requires no architectural modification.
AI.motivation: LLMs treat all context tokens uniformly, which leads to prompt injection vulnerabilities, ambiguous instruction binding and unreliable execution control.
AI.method: A post-training methodology using LLMON (LLM Object Notation), which separates instructions from data and requires explicit identifier-based execution; a 4.6B-token structured corpus spanning general, RAG and tool-calling data, augmented with distractor-infused variants; supervised fine-tuning followed by reinforcement learning on Granite-4.1 base models; attention-based interpretability metrics for diagnosing layer-level failure modes.
AI.result: LLMON-structured supervision reduces attack success rates on indirect prompt-injection benchmarks from 53-100% to 0.02-5.6% while preserving general capabilities; the attention-based metrics reveal how the approach reshapes internal attention patterns at individual layers.
AI.conclusion: Explicit execution semantics can be taught through standard post-training without architectural modification.

title: What Does LOL Measure? Hidden Label Shifts in Low-Light Enhancement Benchmarks
summary: LOL-v1 and LOLv2-Real are the standard benchmarks for supervised low-light image enhancement, and several leading methods ship hand-set test-time adjustments with their evaluation scripts. We audit both benchmarks with 18 public checkpoints of eight methods under one metric implementation that reproduces every published number to within 0.09 dB, and find that their test labels differ from their training labels. (i) The 15 LOL-v1 test labels are rendered differently: the same captures appear in LOLv2 with labels of identical luminance but 1.48x lower saturation, and LOL-v1's own training labels match the LOLv2 rendering; we confirm this on the official release. (ii) The LOLv2-Real test set is the contiguous block of images 690-789, whose labels are 14% darker than the training labels (Cliff's delta = -0.45, p < 1e-12) with no comparable shift in the input statistics we examined; methods trained without any labels score up to 5.5 dB higher on test than on train. (iii) All 15 LOL-v1 test inputs reappear in LOLv2-Real, 12 in its training set. The released test-time settings are consistent with compensating for these shifts. Separating what can be calibrated on training data from what only test-set tuning finds, the test-only residual has median 0.00 dB on LOLv2-Syn, which has no shift, but 0.37 dB on LOL-v1 and 0.92 dB on LOLv2-Real (up to 3.9 dB). Under the shift, test-set checkpoint selection inflates a from-scratch model by 0.9-2.0 dB, and removing the released settings changes which method ranks first. We give concrete reporting recommendations.

AI.tldr: An audit of the LOL-v1 and LOLv2-Real low-light enhancement benchmarks finds that their test labels differ systematically from their training labels, so test-set tuning and checkpoint selection inflate reported scores. The paper gives concrete reporting recommendations.
AI.motivation: LOL-v1 and LOLv2-Real are the standard supervised low-light enhancement benchmarks, and several methods ship hand-set test-time adjustments with their evaluation scripts, so whether published numbers reflect genuine performance is unclear.
AI.method: An audit of both benchmarks with 18 public checkpoints of eight methods under one metric implementation that reproduces every published number to within 0.09 dB; comparison of test and training labels and inputs, including Cliff's delta and p-values; analysis of overlap between LOL-v1 test inputs and LOLv2-Real; separation of what can be calibrated on training data from what only test-set tuning finds.
AI.result: The LOL-v1 test labels are rendered differently from the same captures in LOLv2, with 1.48x lower saturation, while LOL-v1 training labels match the LOLv2 rendering; LOLv2-Real test images 690-789 have labels 14% darker than training labels (Cliff's delta -0.45, p < 1e-12); all 15 LOL-v1 test inputs reappear in LOLv2-Real, 12 of them in its training set; the test-only residual has median 0.00 dB on LOLv2-Syn but 0.37 dB on LOL-v1 and 0.92 dB on LOLv2-Real; test-set checkpoint selection inflates a from-scratch model by 0.9-2.0 dB, and removing the released settings changes which method ranks first.
AI.conclusion: Label shifts and test-set tuning distort low-light enhancement rankings, so reported results should separate training-calibrated components from test-tuned ones.

title: MiniMMD: Minimization of MMD for Sampling, Inference and Integration
summary: Many problems in computational statistics and machine learning can be formulated as approximating a target distribution by minimizing a discrepancy over a restricted class of candidate distributions. This minimum-discrepancy viewpoint appears, for example, in numerical integration, sampling, generative modelling, and statistical inference, but these instances are often studied separately in the literature. This thesis develops the first unified treatment of these many problems through the minimization of the maximum mean discrepancy (MMD), a kernel-based discrepancy between probability measures. The central theme is that MMD is not only a statistically meaningful distance between probability distributions, but also a tractable optimization objective to design practical and efficient algorithms. This thesis summarizes the recent theoretical and empirical advancements of such minimum-MMD based algorithms.

AI.tldr: This thesis gives a unified treatment of numerical integration, sampling, generative modelling and statistical inference as minimization of the maximum mean discrepancy (MMD) over restricted classes of candidate distributions. It argues that MMD is both a meaningful distance between distributions and a tractable objective for practical algorithms.
AI.motivation: Many problems in computational statistics and machine learning are formulated as minimum-discrepancy approximation of a target distribution, but these instances are usually studied separately in the literature.
AI.method: The thesis develops one framework around minimizing MMD, a kernel-based discrepancy between probability measures, to design practical and efficient algorithms.
AI.result: The thesis summarizes recent theoretical and empirical advances of minimum-MMD based algorithms across these problems.
AI.conclusion: MMD serves as a single objective linking previously separate problems, and the thesis consolidates recent progress on minimum-MMD algorithms.

title: On Worst-Case Guarantees for Graph-Based Nearest-Neighbor Search
summary: Graph-based nearest neighbor search algorithms like HNSW, DiskANN, NSG, and others have surged in popularity in recent years due to their excellent empirical performance in comparison to space-partitioning methods like IVF data structures and Locality Sensitive Hashing (LSH). However, in contrast to LSH and related methods, obtaining strong worst-case theoretical guarantees for graph-based search has proven challenging. In this paper, we prove a strong lower bound that helps explain the lack of progress towards such guarantees. We show that no standard graph-based method (any that runs a variant of greedy search on a flat or hierarchical graph) can achieve sublinear query time for approximate nearest neighbor search in Euclidean space, even for an arbitrarily large approximation factor. On the other hand, we prove that sublinear query time is possible if we allow for Steiner points in the search graph. We obtain bounds comparable to LSH, showing e.g., that graph-based search with Steiner points can solve $c$-approximate nearest neighbor search in Euclidean space with query time $\tilde{O}(n^{1/(c-1)})$. We complement this result with initial experiments exploring how Steiner points can be incorporated into practical graph-based methods.

AI.tldr: The paper proves that no standard graph-based method, meaning any variant of greedy search on a flat or hierarchical graph, can achieve sublinear query time for approximate nearest neighbour search in Euclidean space. It shows that sublinear query time becomes possible when Steiner points are allowed in the search graph.
AI.motivation: Graph-based methods such as HNSW, DiskANN and NSG perform strongly in practice, but unlike LSH they have lacked strong worst-case guarantees, and the reason for this lack of progress was unclear.
AI.method: The authors prove a lower bound for greedy search on flat and hierarchical graphs, then analyse graph-based search with Steiner points and compare its bounds with those of LSH, followed by initial experiments.
AI.result: Graph-based search with Steiner points solves c-approximate nearest neighbour search in Euclidean space with query time O~(n^(1/(c-1))), comparable to LSH, and initial experiments explore how Steiner points can be added to practical graph methods.
AI.conclusion: The lower bound explains the absence of worst-case guarantees for standard graph methods, and Steiner points offer a route to LSH-like guarantees.

title: In-Context Learning for Multi-Fidelity Multiscale Model Closure and Cross-Operator Out-Of-Distribution Generalization
summary: Multi-fidelity learning uses low-fidelity information (coarse-scale PDE models) together with limited high-fidelity data (fine-scale solutions) to obtain high-accuracy PDE solutions. It is a data-driven approach to downscale reduced-order models to solve PDEs efficiently and accurately. Standard multi-fidelity learning focuses on one operator or PDE; given a new PDE, retraining using additional coarse-fine solution pairs may be required, which is costly. In this work, we propose an in-context multi-fidelity learning framework for learning multiple multi-fidelity operators with one shared model. The model is trained using paired low- and high-fidelity examples as demonstrations from multiple operators, together with a new coarse-scale solution query, to predict the corresponding fine-scale solution. Once trained, given a new PDE operator, a few (fewer than five) coarse-fine demonstration pairs, and a low-cost coarse query, the model predicts the corresponding fine-scale solution without fine-tuning. When the target operator appears in the training dataset but has a different prediction goal, such as predicting beyond the training time interval, no additional demonstrations are needed. Instead, the model uses training coarse-fine pairs from that PDE and information from other training operators. Testing then only requires generating a low-cost coarse-scale solution query, without fine-tuning. Notably, our smallest model contains only 255,364 trainable parameters, corresponding to approximately 456 parameters per training operator for 560 operators.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes an in-context multi-fidelity learning framework in which one shared model predicts fine-scale PDE solutions for many operators from a few coarse-fine demonstration pairs and a coarse query, without fine-tuning. The smallest model has 255,364 trainable parameters for 560 training operators.
AI.motivation: Standard multi-fidelity learning focuses on one operator or PDE at a time, so a new PDE typically requires costly retraining with additional coarse-fine solution pairs.
AI.method: The shared model is trained on paired low- and high-fidelity demonstrations from multiple operators together with a new coarse-scale query, and at test time it takes fewer than five coarse-fine demonstration pairs and a low-cost coarse query.
AI.result: For a new operator, a few coarse-fine demonstration pairs suffice to predict the fine-scale solution without fine-tuning, and for a training operator with a different goal, such as prediction beyond the training time interval, no extra demonstrations are needed.
AI.conclusion: A single shared model can serve many multi-fidelity operators with very few parameters per operator, reducing the need for retraining on each new PDE.

title: Barren Plateaus in Quantum Linear Combinations: Interference and Lie-Algebraic Control
summary: A coherent sum of quantum circuits introduces interference that can alter the training signal. We distinguish a single linear combination of unitaries (LCU) from a circuit that repeatedly alternates branch operations and ancilla mixing. For a single-pass LCU, independent branches with zero matrix means cannot erase the differentiated branch's gradient variance: the total variance is at least the branch variance times the fourth power of its coefficient magnitude. This bound holds at any gate position and does not require the circuit unitaries to be Haar-random. Beyond this lower bound, we derive exact loss and gradient formulas that quantify the additional contributions from interference between branches. One of these terms depends on relative coefficient phases and vanishes when the branch ensemble is invariant under multiplication by $i \mathbb{I}$; a four-qubit matchgate example shows that it can be nonzero. For repeated interleaving with full special-unitary ancilla control, we determine the generated Lie algebra from the associative algebra of the branches, including the available central phase directions. This control result predicts concentration only with additional assumptions on circuit sampling. Matchgate examples exhibit polynomial single-pass LCU variances and exponential concentration under joint Haar-random sampling. We also derive coefficient-selection rules and bounds for postselection, measurement error, and approximate moments.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that for a single-pass linear combination of unitaries (LCU), gradient variance is at least the branch variance times the fourth power of its coefficient magnitude, and that interference between branches adds further terms. It also determines the Lie algebra generated by repeated interleaving with ancilla control.
AI.motivation: A coherent sum of quantum circuits introduces interference that can alter the training signal, so the gradient behaviour of such sums needs analysis beyond independent-branch assumptions.
AI.method: The authors derive a gradient variance lower bound for single-pass LCUs, exact loss and gradient formulas that include interference terms, and the generated Lie algebra for repeated interleaving with full special-unitary ancilla control, together with coefficient-selection rules.
AI.result: The variance bound holds at any gate position without requiring Haar-random circuit unitaries. One interference term vanishes when the branch ensemble is invariant under multiplication by i times the identity, and a four-qubit matchgate example shows it can be nonzero. Matchgate examples show polynomial single-pass variance but exponential concentration under joint Haar-random sampling.
AI.conclusion: Concentration for repeated interleaving is predicted only under additional assumptions on circuit sampling, and the paper also gives bounds for postselection, measurement error and approximate moments.

title: GearUp: DAG-aware Acceleration for Serverless Inference Serving via Slack-guided Pre-loading
summary: Serverless platforms increasingly host machine learning (ML) inference workflows, modeled as directed acyclic graphs (DAGs) of interdependent functions. Beyond container startup, each ML node must load libraries, model weights, and CUDA kernels before it can run. These costs accumulate along dependent DAG paths and place initialization on the end-to-end critical path. Existing systems optimize one half of this problem. DAG-agnostic pre-loading prepares nodes the request may never reach, wasting host and GPU memory. DAG-aware serving routes and scales whole functions, leaving the loading stages inside a node untouched. This paper presents GearUp, a serverless DAG inference serving system that removes ML-node loading from the end-to-end critical path at low resource cost. GearUp profiles the loading stages of each node and schedules them inside the slack time the DAG exposes, hiding initialization behind upstream execution. It reuses initialized instances within and across requests to avoid redundant cold starts. A probabilistic, traffic-adaptive keep-alive policy sets how long idle instances are retained, balancing memory cost against cold-start risk under bursty load. On the AMBER Alert and FINRA-ML workflows with NVIDIA L40S GPUs, GearUp reduces median end-to-end latency by 64.5% and 75.9% against SMIless, for median speedups of 3.1x and 10.0x over cold execution. Integrated GPU and host memory allocation fall by up to 83.9% and 94.6% against eager pre-loading in InstaInfer. GearUp achieves 4.2x strong scaling on four workers.

AI.tldr: GearUp is a serverless DAG inference serving system that schedules model loading inside the slack time of the workflow, removing ML-node initialization from the end-to-end critical path at low resource cost. On two workflows it reduces median end-to-end latency by 64.5% and 75.9% against SMIless.
AI.motivation: In serverless ML inference workflows, loading libraries, weights and CUDA kernels accumulates along DAG paths, while existing systems either pre-load nodes a request may never reach or route whole functions and leave loading inside each node untouched.
AI.method: GearUp profiles the loading stages of each node, schedules them within the slack exposed by the DAG, reuses initialized instances within and across requests, and applies a probabilistic, traffic-adaptive keep-alive policy that balances memory cost against cold-start risk.
AI.result: On the AMBER Alert and FINRA-ML workflows with NVIDIA L40S GPUs, median end-to-end latency falls by 64.5% and 75.9% against SMIless, with median speedups of 3.1x and 10.0x over cold execution. Integrated GPU and host memory allocation falls by up to 83.9% and 94.6% against eager pre-loading in InstaInfer, and strong scaling reaches 4.2x on four workers.
AI.conclusion: Hiding initialization behind upstream execution and reusing instances reduces latency while limiting the memory cost of pre-loading, making serverless DAG inference more practical.

title: Embodied at Sea: Imitation Learning for Multi-Task Underwater Manipulation
comment: 8 pages, 8 figures. For associated files, see this https URL
summary: Behavior Cloning has demonstrated promising generalization capabilities for robotic manipulation in terrestrial environments. However, marine visual distortions and dynamic currents create a severe domain shift that remains a key bottleneck in adapting generalist architectures to underwater field manipulation. To address this, 1616 episodes of underwater manipulation data were collected in calm and turbulent waters and were used to train 14 generalist Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models (DynamicVLA) with varying proprioception observation configurations. Across three tasks on 1260 gradable on-hardware rollouts in a pool, 10 models outperformed the baseline, with the highest-performing model achieving a 93.3% overall success rate, including partial successes. Results are also introduced from a case study evaluating the performance of a single-task Action Chunking Transformer (ACT) and a generalist VLA (SmolVLA) policy for two tasks in marine archaeology and conservation: grasping and mooring. Experiments are performed on an ROV on and around the WWII wreck Coralita X127 and at Manoel Island Marina, Malta. Across 748 collected episodes and 508 gradable on-hardware rollouts, the ACT policy substantially outperformed SmolVLA (47.9% vs. 7.9% pooled success rate), earning a 66.7% success rate on the most successful task at the marine archaeological site. To enable further contributions to embodied intelligence in marine field robotics, the BLUEMBODIED KIT used to collect data, train models, and deploy policies on the ROV has been open sourced.

AI.tldr: The paper trains 14 generalist Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models on 1616 underwater manipulation episodes, and the best reaches 93.3% overall success on three tasks. A field case study finds that ACT outperforms SmolVLA on marine archaeology and conservation tasks, and the BLUEMBODIED KIT is open-sourced.
AI.motivation: Behaviour cloning generalizes well on land, but marine visual distortion and dynamic currents create a domain shift that limits generalist architectures in underwater field manipulation.
AI.method: The authors collect underwater manipulation data in calm and turbulent waters and train 14 DynamicVLA models with varying proprioception configurations, then deploy a single-task ACT policy and a generalist SmolVLA policy on an ROV for two field tasks.
AI.result: On three tasks with 1260 gradable on-hardware rollouts, 10 models outperform the baseline and the best reaches 93.3% overall success, including partial successes. In the field, ACT achieves 47.9% pooled success against 7.9% for SmolVLA over 508 gradable rollouts, reaching 66.7% on the most successful task.
AI.conclusion: Imitation learning is feasible for underwater manipulation in field settings, and the released kit is intended to support further embodied intelligence research in marine robotics.

title: Skeleton Coding: Program Structure as a Specification for Agents
summary: Coding agents are typically provided end-to-end behavioral specifications that the code they produce should satisfy, such as tests and input--output examples. How many such specifications must a developer provide, and which ones, for the agent to produce the developer's intended program? We argue that this cannot be determined a priori, for it depends on the structure of the implementation, which is left to the agent to decide. An agent first commits to a structure---a decomposition into data types, modules, and functions---which fixes a class of candidate programs; behavioral specifications then select a program within that class. A set of tests that suffices for one structure may leave another badly underdetermined, requiring different edge cases or exponentially more examples. Since the structure is chosen by the agent, developers cannot ensure their specification is complete without reverse-engineering it from thousands of lines of generated code. To resolve this, we introduce Skeleton Coding, in which developers jointly specify the structure---in high-level, code-like format---alongside behavioral specifications. Theoretically, we model AI-assisted coding as a control problem, and show that skeletons can reduce exponentially the number of tests developers must supply to steer an agent toward an acceptable program. Empirically, across four models and three benchmarks, the best-performing skeleton specifications reduce mean test error by 48.4% relative to the best end-to-end behavioral specifications. Even when the agent can query a complete reference implementation, adding a skeleton reduces mean test error relatively by up to 27.0%. Skeletons also narrow the average gap between small and large models by about 52.4% while lowering implementation cost by 15--26x, and reduce code erosion by 24.7% on average.

AI.tldr: Skeleton Coding asks developers to specify the program structure in high-level, code-like form alongside behavioural tests, and shows that skeletons can reduce exponentially the number of tests needed to steer an agent. Across four models and three benchmarks, the best skeletons reduce mean test error by 48.4% relative to the best end-to-end behavioural specifications.
AI.motivation: Coding agents choose their own program structure, so developers cannot know whether their tests and examples are sufficient without reverse-engineering thousands of lines of generated code.
AI.method: The authors model AI-assisted coding as a control problem and introduce Skeleton Coding, in which developers jointly provide a structural skeleton of data types, modules and functions together with behavioural specifications.
AI.result: Across four models and three benchmarks, the best skeletons reduce mean test error by 48.4% relative to the best end-to-end behavioural specifications, and by up to 27.0% even when the agent can query a complete reference implementation. Skeletons also narrow the small-to-large model gap by about 52.4%, lower implementation cost by 15 to 26 times and reduce code erosion by 24.7% on average.
AI.conclusion: Specifying structure alongside behaviour makes it possible to steer agents with far fewer tests, so developer specifications can be complete without inspecting the generated code.

title: The Endgame of FSDP Communication: Layout-Aware Collectives on Copy Engines, RDMA, and NVSwitch
summary: Fully Sharded Data Parallelism (FSDP2) maintains parameters and gradients as per-parameter tensors, whereas its collective path operates on flat, rank-major buffers. Converting between these layouts copies all-gather outputs into parameter storage and packs gradients into full-group fp32 buffers. Layout conversion alone accounts for 6.4% of step time in Llama-3.1 70B training at 8K tokens per GPU. Communication kernels impose a second cost: a default NCCL reduce-scatter can slow a concurrent GEMM that would otherwise complete in a single wave by 69%. We present TIDE, a set of zero-copy collectives built on public NCCL 2.31+ APIs. TIDE preserves FSDP2's per-parameter storage and compute kernels while folding layout placement into collective addressing. TIDE-AG delivers shards directly to parameter storage using NVSwitch multicast and paced recursive-doubling RDMA, with no SMs used for transport or placement. TIDE-RS consumes per-parameter bf16 gradients directly and reduces them into fp32 shards (a mixed-precision mode that NCCL does not provide) using copy engines and short-lived thread blocks (CTAs) for node-local accumulation and NVSwitch for cross-node reduction. A two-phase pipeline separates gradient reads from network progress; Slot-Reuse optionally stages gradients in vacated all-gather slots. On 64 GPUs, TIDE reduces step time by up to 27.1% relative to Stock FSDP2 and 6.0% relative to FSDP2+SymmMem across Llama-3.1 70B, Wan2.2, and Qwen3-30B-A3B. It reduces reduce-scatter SM time by factors of 12.5-14.5 and cuts interference with concurrent compute by up to an order of magnitude. Its reduce-scatter buffer remains nearly constant from 16 to 64 GPUs at a fixed per-GPU output size, and its peak memory is up to 4.7 GiB below FSDP2+SymmMem's and, with Slot-Reuse on Wan2.2, below Stock FSDP2's.

AI.tldr: TIDE is a set of zero-copy collectives built on public NCCL 2.31+ APIs that folds FSDP2 layout conversion into collective addressing. On 64 GPUs it reduces step time by up to 27.1% relative to stock FSDP2 and by 6.0% relative to FSDP2 with SymmMem.
AI.motivation: FSDP2 keeps per-parameter tensors while its collectives operate on flat rank-major buffers, so layout conversion accounts for 6.4% of step time in Llama-3.1 70B training, and a default NCCL reduce-scatter can slow a concurrent GEMM by up to 69%.
AI.method: TIDE-AG delivers all-gather shards directly into parameter storage using NVSwitch multicast and paced recursive-doubling RDMA, and TIDE-RS reduces per-parameter bf16 gradients into fp32 shards using copy engines, short-lived thread blocks and NVSwitch, in a two-phase pipeline with optional Slot-Reuse.
AI.result: On 64 GPUs across Llama-3.1 70B, Wan2.2 and Qwen3-30B-A3B, step time drops by up to 27.1% against stock FSDP2 and 6.0% against FSDP2 with SymmMem. Reduce-scatter SM time falls by factors of 12.5 to 14.5, and peak memory is up to 4.7 GiB below FSDP2 with SymmMem.
AI.conclusion: Layout-aware zero-copy collectives remove layout and communication overhead in FSDP2 training while keeping its per-parameter storage and compute kernels unchanged.

title: A Witnessing Duality for ReLU Network Depth
summary: A depth lower bound for ReLU networks asserts that every shallower network errs on some input; we ask when a weak theory can prove such a bound so that an error can be computed. For the exact computation of $\max(x_1,\ldots,x_n)$, recent work shows two hidden layers suffice with unrestricted rational weights. By contrast, Haase, Hertrich and Loho (ICLR 2023) proved that integer weights require depth logarithmic in $n$, and Averkov, Hojny and Merkert (ICLR 2025) extended the bound to nonbias weights whose denominators are powers of a fixed integer not divisible by a prime $q$. With integer weights the bound is sharp: the classical balanced construction has depth $\lceil\log_2 n\rceil$. For each fixed $q$ and depth cap $K$, we prove this known bound in $\mathbf{VTC}^0$, the bounded-arithmetic theory of uniform constant-depth threshold computation, together with a refuter that is itself such a computation and whose correctness the theory proves. Given a network with at most $K$ hidden layers, nonbias weights whose reduced denominators avoid $q$, arbitrary rational biases and $n>q^K$ inputs, the refuter returns a rational input of polynomial length on which the network errs. The proof makes the obstruction finite: an iterated intersection product of piecewise-linear functions is divisible by $q$ for the network but not for the maximum, so one of finitely many test points exposes the error. By witnessing, provable refutation corresponds to a provably correct refuter, and provable existence of a certified network to a provably correct constructor. On the construction side, we introduce certificates that label each maximum gadget by the inputs it aggregates; with them the theory verifies the balanced construction, which meets the refuter at the sharp threshold $n\le2^K$, and a rational family of polynomial description length and depth $O(\log n/\log\log n)$ built from known depth-two blocks.

AI.tldr: The paper proves in the bounded-arithmetic theory VTC0 the known depth bound for exactly computing the maximum of n inputs with integer weights, together with a provably correct refuter that outputs a polynomial-length rational input on which any shallower network errs. It also gives a provably correct constructor for the balanced network that meets the sharp threshold.
AI.motivation: Known depth lower bounds for ReLU networks computing the maximum are established outside weak theories, so there is no formal guarantee that a witness of error for a shallower network can be computed within such a theory.
AI.method: For each fixed q and depth cap K, the authors prove the bound inside VTC0 using a refuter that is itself a uniform constant-depth threshold computation, an iterated intersection product of piecewise-linear functions that is divisible by q for the network but not for the maximum, and certificates that label each maximum gadget by the inputs it aggregates.
AI.result: Given a network with at most K hidden layers, nonbias weights whose reduced denominators avoid q and n greater than q^K inputs, the refuter returns a rational input of polynomial length on which the network errs. The theory verifies the balanced construction at the sharp threshold n at most 2^K and a rational family of depth O(log n / log log n) built from depth-two blocks.
AI.conclusion: Provable refutation corresponds to a provably correct refuter and provable existence of a certified network to a provably correct constructor, giving a witnessing duality for ReLU network depth.

title: Does 3D Pose Improve Action Valuation in Football? An Empirical Study of Pose Representations and Learning Objectives
summary: Football action valuation estimates players' contributions to future scoring. Existing multi-agent deep reinforcement learning (MADRL) models use 2D positions and velocities, omitting posture information relevant to imminent actions. We investigate whether adding 3D pose to a SARSA-based model improves observed-action values relative to attack returns: goals, conceded goals or final expected possession value. Using UEFA Champions League 2022/23 event, tracking and 3D pose data, we compare six representations (no pose, raw joints, torso and head orientation, and spatial-temporal graph convolutional network (ST-GCN) embeddings) across five learning settings and three seeds. The settings vary temporal-difference targets and action-prediction loss, with Monte Carlo return regression as a reference. Across 50 on-ball and off-ball comparisons, pose robustly improved return prediction in only three, all using torso and head orientation, while worsening it in twelve, mostly with ST-GCN. Training choices had greater effects: removing the action-prediction loss raised on-ball skill of position-only values from 0.003 to 0.040 and their correlation with expected goals from 0.23 to 0.60; the improvement in return prediction persisted at matched training length. Separately, pose improved prediction of the on-ball action 0.2 s ahead (macro AUC 0.914 to 0.934 with raw joints), while the passer's pose during execution improved pass-success prediction (AUC 0.844 to 0.856). Within this training protocol, pose informed imminent actions but rarely improved observed-action values.

AI.tldr: The study tests whether adding 3D pose to a SARSA-based multi-agent model improves football action valuation, and finds that pose rarely improves observed-action values despite gains in predicting imminent actions. Training choices have larger effects than the choice of pose representation.
