summary: Radio-frequency (RF) sensing enables robot ego-motion estimation in darkness, smoke, and fog, yet RF odometry remains challenging because multipath and moving reflectors make cross-frame matching highly ambiguous. Existing methods often rely on auxiliary inertial sensors or ground-truth pose supervision. We present RFWalk, a self-supervised, RF-only odometry framework that models dense correspondences across range-azimuth frames as random walks on a space-time graph and learns them from unlabeled sequences through temporal cycle consistency. To rule out correspondences that are cycle-consistent but physically implausible, we introduce a Doppler consistency loss that constrains correspondence-induced motion using radial velocity measured by the RF sensor itself. Ego-motion is then recovered through robust $\mathrm{SE}(2)$ registration that suppresses uncertain correspondences and those arising from independently moving objects. Without pose labels or auxiliary sensors, RFWalk remains competitive with supervised baselines in static scenes and reduces absolute trajectory error by 58% in dynamic scenes with moving pedestrians.

AI.tldr: RFWalk is a self-supervised, RF-only odometry method that learns dense correspondences through temporal cycle consistency with a Doppler consistency loss, reducing absolute trajectory error by 58% in dynamic scenes.
AI.motivation: RF odometry is ambiguous because of multipath and moving reflectors, and existing methods rely on auxiliary inertial sensors or ground-truth pose supervision.
AI.method: Models correspondences across range-azimuth frames as random walks on a space-time graph, trained with temporal cycle consistency; a Doppler consistency loss uses the sensor's radial velocity to rule out physically implausible correspondences; ego-motion is recovered by robust SE(2) registration.
AI.result: Without pose labels or auxiliary sensors, RFWalk remains competitive with supervised baselines in static scenes and reduces absolute trajectory error by 58% in dynamic scenes with moving pedestrians.
AI.conclusion: Physically grounded RF-only ego-motion estimation is feasible without labels or extra sensors, which matters for robots operating in darkness, smoke and fog.

title: Blind Spots: Where Small Language Models Fall Behind Frontier Models on Terminal Tasks
summary: Small language models (SLMs) offer an attractive alternative to frontier models (FMs) because they can be deployed with lower cost and latency. This makes SLMs especially appealing for terminal tasks on edge devices, where responsiveness, local execution, and limited connectivity are important considerations. However, they continue to lag behind FMs on terminal tasks, as measured by standard task success rates. Yet these rates conflate several capabilities that may contribute to this gap. In this work, we characterize the SLM-FM gap along three axes: solvability, whether additional test-time compute allows an SLM to reach a correct solution; verification, whether it can identify a successful solution among candidate trajectories; and confidence, whether it can accurately anticipate its probability of success. Across two standard terminal benchmarks, we find that repeated sampling narrows, but does not eliminate, the gap in solvability. In contrast, a persistent gap remains in verification. Given the same candidate trajectory pool, FMs recover substantially more of the gap between random and oracle selection than SLMs. SLMs are also more overconfident in their prospective success estimates and exhibit poorer calibration. These results suggest that the SLM-FM gap is multidimensional, spanning not only the ability to generate successful solutions, but also the ability to recognize successful solutions and anticipate success. We hope this decomposition can guide future work on developing stronger and smaller terminal agents.

AI.tldr: Decomposes the small-versus-frontier language model gap on terminal tasks into solvability, verification and confidence, finding that repeated sampling narrows the solvability gap but a persistent gap remains in verification and calibration.
AI.motivation: Standard task success rates conflate several capabilities, so the reason small language models lag behind frontier models on terminal tasks is unclear.
AI.method: Characterizes the gap along three axes: solvability, meaning whether extra test-time compute lets an SLM reach a correct solution; verification, meaning whether it can pick a successful trajectory from a candidate pool; and confidence, meaning whether it can anticipate its probability of success. Evaluated on two standard terminal benchmarks.
AI.result: Repeated sampling narrows but does not eliminate the solvability gap, while a persistent gap remains in verification. Given the same candidate pool, frontier models recover substantially more of the gap between random and oracle selection. SLMs are more overconfident and exhibit poorer calibration.
AI.conclusion: The SLM-FM gap spans the ability to generate, to recognize, and to anticipate success, and this decomposition can guide the development of stronger and smaller terminal agents.

title: Formal Specifications with Data-Driven Signal Analysis
summary: Developing analog and hybrid systems requires substantial domain knowledge that is hard to articulate in a formal specification; without additional effort, this domain knowledge is also inaccessible to machine learning methods. We propose a hybrid approach for analyzing and monitoring real-valued signals that integrates specification-based and data-driven techniques. We use regular expressions with interval operations to identify regions of interest in a signal, classical signal processing methods to extract semantically meaningful features, and semi-supervised machine learning to infer complex relationships that distinguish correct from faulty behaviors. The relationships learned from normal behavior data can automatically detect incorrect behavior in the same system or variants thereof. We evaluate the method on a voltage regulator, demonstrating its effectiveness in detecting undesired system behaviors.

AI.tldr: Proposes a hybrid method for analyzing real-valued signals that combines regular-expression region-of-interest detection, classical signal-processing features and semi-supervised learning to detect faulty behavior, demonstrated on a voltage regulator.
AI.motivation: Developing analog and hybrid systems requires domain knowledge that is hard to express as a formal specification, so machine learning methods cannot access it.
AI.method: Regular expressions with interval operations identify regions of interest in a signal, classical signal-processing methods extract semantically meaningful features, and semi-supervised learning infers relationships that separate correct from faulty behavior using normal-behavior data.
AI.result: The relationships learned from normal behavior detect incorrect behavior in the same system or its variants; the method is shown to be effective in detecting undesired behaviors of a voltage regulator. No quantitative results are given in the abstract.
AI.conclusion: Combining specification-based and data-driven techniques makes domain knowledge usable by machine learning and enables automatic detection of incorrect system behavior.

title: The Search for Statistical Indistinguishability Between Real and Fake Images
summary: Images produced by generative models appear strikingly similar to real ones. In this work, we study whether perfection has been reached by generated content in terms of matching the properties of real data. We train deep neural networks to separate real data from fake and observe their test accuracies. Only a chance performance has any scope of proving statistical indistinguishability. However, since generative models are known to sometimes introduce small errors, e.g., low level checkerboard artifacts, we create progressive abstractions of the original real/fake images to potentially bring them to a space where those artifacts get wiped away. These include operations such as blurring, downsizing, cropping, converting RGB images into edge/semantic maps, etc. To our surprise, almost none of the abstractions are able to make fake data indistinguishable from real. The only cases when neural network based classifiers fail to separate the two categories is when the data is abstracted to such an extent that the original content seems mostly lost to the human eye, e.g., downsizing a $256 \times 256$ RGB image of human face to $4 \times 4$ resolution. We observe this trend across four different datasets of varying complexity (MNIST, CelebA, FFHQ and GenImage) and across various types of generative models (GANs, VAEs, diffusion models). This shows that the nature of fake artifacts extends all the way from low level to very high level in images. The simple implication is that fake images are much more different from real than we are used to think.

AI.tldr: The paper tests whether generated images become statistically indistinguishable from real ones by training classifiers to separate real from fake images after progressive abstraction (blurring, downsizing, cropping, edge or semantic maps). Almost all abstractions still leave fakes separable, and only extreme abstraction, such as downsizing faces to 4x4, removes the distinction.
AI.motivation: Generated images look strikingly realistic, but it is unclear whether they match real data in their statistical properties, since small low-level artifacts such as checkerboard patterns may still reveal them.
AI.method: Deep networks are trained to separate real from fake images, and their test accuracy is measured after progressive abstractions intended to wipe away low-level artifacts, including blurring, downsizing, cropping, and conversion to edge or semantic maps. Experiments span MNIST, CelebA, FFHQ, and GenImage with GANs, VAEs, and diffusion models.
AI.result: Almost no abstraction makes fake data indistinguishable from real. Classifiers fail only when the data is abstracted so heavily that the content is largely lost to the human eye, such as downsizing 256x256 RGB face images to 4x4. The trend holds across all four datasets and all three types of generative model.
AI.conclusion: Fake artifacts extend from low level to very high level in images, so fake images differ from real ones much more than commonly assumed.

title: MCCL: Training Pytorch models across a fleet of Macs at Skywalker Sound
summary: Skywalker Sound, a premier audio post-production facility, operates more than 200 M4 Max Mac Studios on a 10Gb Ethernet network. When not in use by artists, these machines sit idle, representing massive untapped unified memory and compute capacity. While these fleets are excellent candidates for distributed machine learning alongside existing NVIDIA GPU clusters, PyTorch lacks an accelerated distributed backend for Apple's Metal Performance Shaders (MPS). To bridge this gap, we introduce the Metal Communication Collective Library (MCCL), the first open-source MPS backend for multi-node PyTorch training over switched Ethernet. We evaluate its performance and scalability across 24 nodes, demonstrating that large all-reduce operations reach 98-99.7% of TCP goodput. Training a 113.5M-parameter Vision Transformer (ViT) scales from 198 to 4,568 samples/s, achieving 95.9% parallel efficiency. Benchmarked against an NVIDIA A100 GPU, one M4 Max Mac equals roughly 1.7x the throughput of FP32 matrix multiplication, and 5.5 Macs match an A100 using TF32. Harnessing 100 idle Macs for 12 hours nightly offsets approximately $200,000 annually in equivalent cloud compute costs. Our results demonstrate that existing Mac infrastructure can be seamlessly repurposed for high performance distributed training without abandoning the standard PyTorch codebase.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces MCCL, an open-source Metal (MPS) communication backend that enables multi-node PyTorch training across a fleet of Mac Studios over Ethernet. Across 24 nodes it reaches near-line-rate all-reduce throughput and 95.9% parallel efficiency when training a ViT.
AI.motivation: PyTorch has no accelerated distributed backend for Apple's Metal Performance Shaders, so the idle unified memory and compute of large Mac fleets in studios such as Skywalker Sound cannot be used for distributed training alongside NVIDIA GPU clusters.
AI.method: The authors build MCCL, the Metal Communication Collective Library, as the first open-source MPS backend for multi-node PyTorch training over switched 10Gb Ethernet, keeping the standard PyTorch codebase.
AI.result: On 24 nodes, large all-reduce operations reach 98-99.7% of TCP goodput. Training a 113.5M-parameter ViT scales from 198 to 4,568 samples/s, a 95.9% parallel efficiency. One M4 Max Mac gives roughly 1.7x the FP32 matrix multiplication throughput of an NVIDIA A100, and 5.5 Macs match an A100 using TF32.
AI.conclusion: Existing Mac infrastructure can be repurposed for high-performance distributed training; using 100 idle Macs for 12 hours nightly offsets about $200,000 per year in equivalent cloud compute.

title: Modular Bayesian Foundation Models: Bayesian time series encoders for OOD detection, routing and forecasting
summary: Industrial systems continuously generate time series that vary in sampling frequency, scale, dynamics, and operating regime. Consequently a single time-series foundation model may not be able to represent all regimes effectively and retraining a large model for every new dataset or regime shift is computationally expensive. Modular foundation models address this issue by reusing specialised encoders trained on diverse datasets and by allowing the expansion of capabilities through the addition of new experts. This approach requires compact experts to minimize storage cost and a proper selection mechanism of experts for unseen data. We propose a modular foundation model framework that combines end-to-end Bayesian encoder training with uncertainty based routing. Using Singular Bayesian Neural Networks (SBNNs), we build a collection of compact Bayesian encoders whose epistemic uncertainty guides label-free selection. At the selected ranks, our Bayesian collection uses 63.8\% less storage than its deterministic counterpart. We evaluate this framework on time-series data through distribution shift, encoder selection, and probabilistic forecasting. Across seven incoming datasets, uncertainty-based routing is competitive with distance-based routing in terms of forecast MSE, while reducing average ECE from 0.086 to 0.072 and average NLL from 0.907 to 0.836. It also increases PICP90 from 82.28\% to 89.03\%. In a separate model-family comparison, we evaluate the SBNN pipeline against full-rank Bayes by Backprop, deep ensembles, and MC Dropout. The SBNN pipeline achieves an average MSE of 0.390, comparable with 0.396 for deep ensembles, 0.389 for MC dropout, and 0.443 for the full-rank Bayesian model. It uses 63.9\% fewer parameters than MC dropout, 81.9\% fewer than the full-rank model, and 92.8\% fewer than the deep ensemble.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a modular time-series foundation model built from compact Bayesian encoders (Singular Bayesian Neural Networks) whose epistemic uncertainty drives label-free expert selection. It matches the accuracy of deterministic routing with less storage and is competitive with strong uncertainty baselines in forecasting.
AI.motivation: A single time-series foundation model may not represent all industrial regimes, and retraining a large model for every new dataset or regime shift is expensive, so modular experts must be compact and must be selected reliably for unseen data.
AI.method: End-to-end Bayesian encoder training is combined with uncertainty-based routing. Singular Bayesian Neural Networks give a collection of compact Bayesian encoders whose epistemic uncertainty guides label-free selection of experts, evaluated on distribution shift, encoder selection, and probabilistic forecasting.
AI.result: At the selected ranks the Bayesian collection uses 63.8% less storage than its deterministic counterpart. Across seven incoming datasets, uncertainty-based routing is competitive with distance-based routing on forecast MSE, lowers average ECE from 0.086 to 0.072 and average NLL from 0.907 to 0.836, and raises PICP90 from 82.28% to 89.03%. The SBNN pipeline reaches average MSE 0.390, comparable with deep ensembles (0.396) and MC Dropout (0.389), and uses 63.9%, 81.9%, and 92.8% fewer parameters than MC Dropout, full-rank Bayes by Backprop, and deep ensembles, respectively.
AI.conclusion: Uncertainty-based routing with compact Bayesian encoders offers a parameter- and storage-efficient route to modular, better-calibrated time-series foundation models for industrial settings.

title: Tabular foundation models are not a shortcut to calibrated clinical risk prediction: a pre-registered simulation against the true risk
comment: 37 pages, 7 figures, 1 table; Supplementary Information (55 pages) as an ancillary file. Pre-registered on OSF Registries (doi:https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/8HMTZ). Code: doi:https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23737378%3B benchmark data: doi:https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23737416
summary: Tabular foundation models are pretrained networks that predict risk from a table without fitting a model. Whether their risks are correct (calibrated) has been judged on real data, where true risk is unknown. In a pre-registered simulation with known true risks, we compared TabPFN-3.5, TabICLv2 and Mitra-v2 with Firth logistic regression with intercept correction (FLIC) in 58 scenarios and 1,000 random designs, then on four clinical data sets. Foundation models were not a shortcut to calibration. Their calibration slope matched FLIC's within the pre-registered margin in 36 or 37 of 48 core scenarios and was better only at n = 200 with a 3% event rate. Even 3,000 patients were often not enough: with FLIC, TabPFN-3.5 or Mitra-v2, 63%-83% of samples gave risks close to the truth in average, intercept and slope at event rates of 10% and 30%, and 35%-50% at 3%. TabICLv2 did worse (8%-39% and 1%-3%). Across the random designs, foundation models had a lower true calibration error than FLIC beyond the margin in 25%-38% and a higher one in none, though small losses were predicted at n = 3000. On real data, no model resisted a change in event rate between populations; recalibration on 500 local patients largely repaired it.

AI.tldr: In a pre-registered simulation with known true risks, tabular foundation models (TabPFN-3.5, TabICLv2, Mitra-v2) are not a shortcut to calibrated clinical risk prediction: their calibration matched Firth logistic regression with intercept correction (FLIC) in most core scenarios. Even with FLIC or the foundation models, thousands of patients are often needed for reliable calibration at low event rates.
AI.motivation: Tabular foundation models have been judged for calibration only on real data, where the true risk is unknown, so their calibration quality for clinical risk prediction remained unclear.
AI.method: A pre-registered simulation with known true risks compares TabPFN-3.5, TabICLv2, and Mitra-v2 with FLIC over 58 scenarios and 1,000 random designs, followed by evaluation on four clinical datasets.
AI.result: The calibration slope of the foundation models matched FLIC within the pre-registered margin in 36 or 37 of 48 core scenarios, and was better only at n = 200 with a 3% event rate. Even with 3,000 patients, 63%-83% of samples gave risks close to the truth in average, intercept, and slope for FLIC, TabPFN-3.5, or Mitra-v2 at event rates of 10% and 30%, and 35%-50% at 3%; TabICLv2 did worse. On real data, no model resisted a change in event rate between populations, and recalibration on 500 local patients largely repaired it.
AI.conclusion: Foundation models offer no calibration shortcut for clinical risk prediction, and local recalibration on a modest sample remains necessary when event rates shift between populations.

title: PhysicsNeMo-Mesh: GPU-Native Meshes and Simulation Cases for Physics AI
summary: PhysicsNeMo-Mesh is the mesh module of the open-source PhysicsNeMo library. It provides mesh processing similar to PyVista, but on the GPU, in batches, and inside PyTorch's automatic differentiation. Like xarray for unstructured meshes, it attaches semantics to data: fields on points, cells, and whole meshes have names and shapes, and a simulation case keeps the complete PDE problem specification, including boundary conditions and their prescribed values. It addresses three problems that plague machine learning for physical simulation. First, GPU utilization is bottlenecked by I/O, because samples are very large relative to the compute per forward pass. Second, because traditional preprocessing is expensive, it is necessarily done once, during curation, rather than differently for each model and workflow at the point of use. Finally, advanced equivariant and mesh-native architectures require information that curation ordinarily discards. Fast GPU mesh processing makes it practical to preprocess at the point of use: on one GB200 GPU, mesh operations run $6.2\text{--}1{,}068\times$ faster than VTK with 72 threads, and loading a whole case is $8.0\text{--}88\times$ faster than reading its VTK files ($8.0\times$ when both read the same fields). Overlapped with training, this preprocessing costs $2.1\%$ of throughput for a $127\,\text{ms}$ Transolver step. So one dataset serves many models and workflows: in PhysicsNeMo's public recipe, one stored DrivAerML dataset feeds Transolver, GeoTransolver, and GLOBE. PhysicsNeMo-Mesh combines the speed of an intermediate array store with the flexibility of an archival format such as VTK. When shapes and wall conditions both vary, per-boundary conditions cut a heat-conduction error from $87\%$ to $6\text{--}9\%$. And by keeping field ranks and named boundaries, it retains the semantic structure that next-generation architectures will need.

AI.tldr: PhysicsNeMo-Mesh is a GPU-native mesh module for physics AI that provides batched, differentiable mesh processing with named fields and complete simulation case specifications. It makes preprocessing at the point of use practical and speeds up mesh operations and case loading by large factors relative to VTK.
AI.motivation: Machine learning for physical simulation is limited by I/O on very large samples, by expensive preprocessing that is done once during curation, and by curation that discards information needed by equivariant and mesh-native architectures.
AI.method: The module offers PyVista-like mesh processing on the GPU, in batches, and inside PyTorch automatic differentiation, with xarray-like semantics that name fields on points, cells, and whole meshes, and a simulation case that stores the full PDE problem specification including boundary conditions.
AI.result: On one GB200 GPU, mesh operations run 6.2-1,068x faster than VTK with 72 threads, and loading a whole case is 8.0-88x faster than reading its VTK files (8.0x when both read the same fields). Overlapped with training, preprocessing costs 2.1% of throughput for a 127 ms Transolver step. One stored DrivAerML dataset feeds Transolver, GeoTransolver, and GLOBE. With varying shapes and wall conditions, per-boundary conditions reduce a heat-conduction error from 87% to 6-9%.
AI.conclusion: Combining the speed of an intermediate array store with the flexibility of an archival format lets one dataset serve many models, and keeping field ranks and named boundaries preserves the structure that next-generation architectures need.

title: Tactus: Tactile & Pose Sensing Glove for Natural Dexterity Data Collection
summary: Collecting naturalistic human manipulation demonstrations with accurate contact force and hand pose is essential for robot dexterous manipulation policy and foundational world model learning - yet no existing wearable platform provides both calibrated fingertip force sensing and occlusion-resilient hand tracking in a form factor that preserves natural manipulation behavior. We present Tactus, a textile-integrated sensing glove that co-optimizes three design pillars: (1) a thin, conformal 3D-knit form factor (1.5 mm fingertip stackup) designed to minimize interference with natural manipulation, (2) strategically placed capacitive tactile sensors at manipulation-relevant regions informed by empirical contact studies, and (3) IMU-fused pose tracking that maintains accuracy through the hand-object occlusions where manipulation data is most valuable. Tactus includes a documented calibration pipeline for cross-glove consistency and per-session calibration for subject-dependent correction. To enable objective comparison, we introduce standardized benchmarking protocols for tactile force regression and hand pose estimation, and apply them to Tactus and two commercially available tactile gloves - to our knowledge the first quantitative cross-platform evaluation of this kind. Tactus resolves a minimum detectable force of 0.59 N at 95% confidence, 1.6 - 2.7x lower than the commercial baselines, and with 0.87 cross-participant consistency, while our pose tracking sustains 11.0 mm fingertip keypoint relative error during manipulation, when occlusion is heaviest. We show that these combined signals support object property estimation, slip detection, and representative recording of hand-object interaction - yielding demonstration data with the fidelity required for contact-aware manipulation policies and world models.

AI.tldr: Tactus is a textile-integrated glove that combines calibrated capacitive fingertip force sensing with IMU-fused hand pose tracking to collect dexterous manipulation demonstrations. It shows a lower minimum detectable force than two commercial tactile gloves in the first quantitative cross-platform benchmark of this kind.
AI.motivation: Existing wearable platforms do not provide both calibrated fingertip force sensing and occlusion-resilient hand tracking in a form factor that preserves natural manipulation, and robot dexterous learning needs both.
AI.method: The glove has a thin, conformal 3D-knit form factor (1.5 mm fingertip stackup), capacitive tactile sensors at manipulation-relevant regions, and IMU-fused pose tracking, together with a documented calibration pipeline and standardized benchmarks for tactile force regression and hand pose estimation applied to Tactus and two commercial gloves.
AI.result: Tactus resolves a minimum detectable force of 0.59 N at 95% confidence, 1.6-2.7x lower than the commercial baselines, with 0.87 cross-participant consistency. Pose tracking sustains 11.0 mm fingertip keypoint relative error during the heaviest occlusion. The combined signals support object property estimation, slip detection, and representative recording of hand-object interaction.
AI.conclusion: Tactus provides demonstration data with the fidelity required for contact-aware manipulation policies and world models.

title: PALATE: Pretrained Autoregressive LATent Embeddings
comment: Accepted to GRAIL @ CIKM 2026. 5 pages, 2 figures, 3 tables
summary: Local-commerce and food-delivery marketplaces run large ads businesses: across hundreds of thousands of stores, merchants pay to be surfaced on browse and search surfaces, and a ranker decides which ads each consumer sees. Ranking well demands strong per-consumer personalization, yet a consumer's raw interaction history is sparse and high-cardinality. Our production ranker had personalized only through hand-engineered signals: aggregate engagement counts, categorical embeddings, and order-agnostic pooled history, with no learned per-consumer sequence representation. We learn one by training a GPT-style generative model of the consumer's engagement sequence to predict their next few engagements, and read its last-token hidden state as the consumer embedding. That single frozen vector becomes one shared personalization input for every ad surface: a daily job refreshes it, and each ranker consumes it as an ordinary dense feature. Offline it is the largest single-feature gain in our ranking-AUC ladder, a relative Eval-AUC gain of +0.59% on a browse-driven feed and +0.57% on a query-driven search surface. Online, it shipped as one component of bundled ranker retrains on both surfaces: Discovery (revenue +0.79%, conversion rate +1.17%) and Search (revenue +0.94%, conversion rate +1.50%). Three design choices adapt the generative objective to a repurchase-heavy marketplace, and are the core of our contribution: an exploration-weighted loss that up-weights businesses new to the consumer over ones already engaged; a two-stage curriculum: a click pretrain that keeps the representation broad and exploratory, then a conversion fine-tune that sharpens purchase intent; and a designed negative set that pairs a fixed popular-business pool and businesses shown but not ordered with random and in-batch negatives.

AI.tldr: PALATE learns a consumer embedding by training a GPT-style generative model on engagement sequences and using its last-token hidden state as a frozen personalization feature for ad rankers. It gives the largest single-feature offline gain in the ranking-AUC ladder and shipped online with revenue and conversion lifts on two surfaces.
AI.motivation: Production ad rankers used only hand-engineered signals, such as aggregate engagement counts, categorical embeddings, and order-agnostic pooled history, with no learned per-consumer sequence representation, while raw interaction histories are sparse and high-cardinality.
AI.method: A GPT-style model is trained to predict a consumer's next few engagements, and its last-token hidden state, refreshed daily, serves as a frozen dense feature for all ad surfaces. Three design choices adapt the objective to a repurchase-heavy marketplace: an exploration-weighted loss that up-weights businesses new to the consumer, a two-stage click-pretrain then conversion-fine-tune curriculum, and a designed negative set mixing popular and shown-but-not-ordered businesses with random and in-batch negatives.
AI.result: Offline relative Eval-AUC gains are +0.59% on a browse-driven feed and +0.57% on a query-driven search surface. Online, as part of bundled ranker retrains, Discovery improved revenue by 0.79% and conversion rate by 1.17%, and Search improved revenue by 0.94% and conversion rate by 1.50%.
AI.conclusion: A frozen generative sequence embedding is an effective shared personalization signal for ad ranking, and the three objective adaptations are the core of the contribution for repurchase-heavy marketplaces.

title: DICE: Decentralized Incentive-driven Federated Learning for Efficient & Scalable Customization of Pretrained Models in Web3
summary: Customizing Pretrained Models (PMs) for downstream tasks demands task-specific data, which burgeoning Web3 applications provide abundantly. Blockchain-powered federated learning (BCFL) offers a secure and privacy-preserving paradigm to customize PMs among self-interested and untrusted Web3 participants. Yet, existing BCFL algorithms face severe efficiency and scalability challenges when applied to large PMs, due to their substantial computational and memory requirements and the hardware constraints of many participants. This paper introduces DICE, a novel BCFL algorithm that addresses the efficiency and scalability challenges of customizing large PMs in Web3 via two sets of synergistic techniques: (i) a dynamic progressive learning scheme and a model slice verification scheme to enable a wider range of honest participants, including those unable to deploy the full model, to engage in customizing PMs, while preserving model utility; (ii) a tree-structured committee consensus protocol and an efficiency-driven incentive scheme to address the dominant bottleneck that hinders existing BCFL algorithms from scaling to a larger number of data holders for customizing data-hungry large PMs, while maintaining security. Theoretical analysis and extensive experimental results on customizing vision and language PMs demonstrate DICE's efficiency, effectiveness, and security.

AI.tldr: DICE is a blockchain-powered federated learning algorithm that customizes large pretrained models among untrusted Web3 participants, including those unable to host the full model. It combines progressive learning and model slice verification with a tree-structured committee consensus and efficiency-driven incentives.
AI.motivation: Existing blockchain federated learning algorithms face efficiency and scalability problems with large pretrained models because of their computational and memory requirements and the limited hardware of many participants.
AI.method: Two synergistic techniques are used: a dynamic progressive learning scheme with model slice verification, so that participants who cannot deploy the full model can still contribute, and a tree-structured committee consensus protocol with an efficiency-driven incentive scheme that scales to more data holders.
AI.result: Theoretical analysis and experiments on customizing vision and language pretrained models demonstrate efficiency, effectiveness, and security. The abstract reports no specific numerical results.
AI.conclusion: DICE enables scalable and secure customization of large pretrained models in Web3 with a wider range of honest participants while preserving model utility.

title: Learning Erasing Equal-Length Relational Pattern Languages in the Limit from Positive Data over Binary Alphabets
summary: Relational pattern languages generalize Angluin's pattern languages by requiring the strings substituted for repeated occurrences of a variable to stand in a given relation, rather than to be identical. We study erasing pattern languages under the equal-length relation, where all occurrences of a variable must be replaced by strings of the same length. Over alphabets with at least three letters, this class is known to be learnable in the limit from positive data. We show that over a binary alphabet it is not, which resolves an open question from earlier work. Our proof reveals that non-learnability already holds for the restricted subclass of languages generated by patterns that have exactly three maximal substrings of variables. We then show that patterns with at most two maximal substrings of variables are learnable in the limit from positive data for every alphabet of size at least two. If the target pattern is known to have at most one maximal substring of variables, this can even be achieved by an iterative learner, which updates its hypothesis using only the current example and its previous hypothesis.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that erasing pattern languages under the equal-length relation are not learnable in the limit from positive data over a binary alphabet, which resolves an open question. It identifies learnable subclasses: patterns with at most two maximal variable substrings are learnable for every alphabet of size at least two, and an iterative learner suffices when at most one is known.
AI.motivation: Relational pattern languages generalize Angluin's pattern languages; learnability was known for alphabets with at least three letters, but the binary case was an open question from earlier work.
AI.method: A learning-theoretic analysis of erasing pattern languages under the equal-length relation. A non-learnability proof for patterns with exactly three maximal variable substrings over binary alphabets is complemented by learning algorithms for patterns with at most two such substrings.
AI.result: Over binary alphabets the class is not learnable in the limit from positive data, already for patterns with exactly three maximal substrings of variables. Patterns with at most two maximal substrings of variables are learnable in the limit from positive data for every alphabet of size at least two, and an iterative learner suffices when at most one is known.
AI.conclusion: Over binary alphabets, learnability holds for at most two maximal variable substrings and already fails at three, which settles the open question for the binary case.

title: EmbodiExp: Compositional Experience Transfer for Embodied Agents
summary: Experience can help embodied agents turn high-level plans into grounded actions, but transferring it across tasks remains challenging: previously effective strategies may be inapplicable to the current state or fail to produce their intended outcomes. We present EmbodiExp, a framework for constructing transferable experiences and composing them online during embodied task execution. Our key observation is that tasks often share subgoals whose completion can be assessed independently of overall task success. We therefore introduce an outcome-grounded subgoal experience that specifies a subgoal, applicability conditions, an adaptable policy, and a verifiable outcome. During execution, applicable experiences guide action generation, while verified outcomes can establish the conditions required by subsequent experiences, enabling online composition. Subgoal-level outcome attribution further enables failure utilization: failed trajectories can still contribute verified local successes and condition-specific guidance on actions to avoid. Experiments on multiple embodied benchmarks under a fold-based protocol with frozen experience banks demonstrate the effectiveness of EmbodiExp.

AI.tldr: EmbodiExp constructs transferable subgoal experiences, each with applicability conditions, an adaptable policy, and a verifiable outcome, and composes them online during embodied task execution. It also learns from failed trajectories by keeping verified local successes and condition-specific guidance on actions to avoid.
AI.motivation: Experience can help embodied agents turn high-level plans into grounded actions, but transferring it across tasks is hard because previously effective strategies may not apply to the current state or may fail to produce their intended outcomes.
AI.method: Outcome-grounded subgoal experiences specify a subgoal, applicability conditions, an adaptable policy, and a verifiable outcome. Applicable experiences guide action generation, verified outcomes establish the conditions needed by later experiences, and subgoal-level outcome attribution enables failure utilization. Evaluation uses a fold-based protocol with frozen experience banks.
AI.result: Experiments on multiple embodied benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness of EmbodiExp. The abstract reports no specific numerical results.
AI.conclusion: Compositional, outcome-verified subgoal experiences make experience transferable across embodied tasks and make failed executions useful as a source of verified local progress.

title: Zero-Complement Extrapolation: Parameter Recovery and Classification in Severely Imbalanced Logistic Regression under Rank-Deficient Regimes
comment: Submitted to a peer-reviewed journal; 16 pages, 1 figure, 4 tables
summary: Parameter estimation and classification in binary logistic regression deteriorate severely when the number of minority class observations ($n_1$) is smaller than the feature dimension ($p$). Under such rank-deficient rarity ($n_1 < p$), maximum likelihood estimators suffer from quasi-complete separation, penalized likelihood methods exhibit severe intercept bias, and convex minority oversampling techniques such as SMOTE collapse into an $(n_1 - 1)$-dimensional affine subspace. In this paper, we propose a novel \textit{Self-Calibrated Zero-Complement} estimator that shifts the paradigm from minority interpolation to majority fringe extrapolation. Grounded in Stein's Lemma, we prove that the conditional expectation shift of the abundant majority class ($Y=0$) induced by logistic truncation uniquely identifies the true hyperplane normal $\boldsymbol{\beta}$ after Mahalanobis whitening. We further establish that extrapolating synthetic minority instances outward from the high-quantile density fringe of the majority distribution along the conjugate direction preserves full-rank covariance regularity ($\mathrm{rank} = p$). To accommodate both semi-supervised environments (with an unlabeled background mean) and strictly supervised subsamples, we introduce a hybrid estimator incorporating the intrinsic third-moment skewness of the majority class alongside a location-shift-invariant zero-boundary intercept calibration. Extensive Monte Carlo simulations and real-world benchmark applications (Wisconsin Diagnostic Breast Cancer and Banknote Authentication) under extreme rarity ($n_1 \in \{3, 5\}$) demonstrate that our approach prevents parameter divergence, recovers the oracle hyperplane with high fidelity, and substantially outperforms Firth's regression and SMOTE in F1-score and estimation stability.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a Self-Calibrated Zero-Complement estimator for logistic regression when the minority class is smaller than the feature dimension, extrapolating synthetic minority points outward from the majority-class fringe. It preserves full-rank covariance and outperforms Firth regression and SMOTE in F1-score and estimation stability on simulations and two benchmarks.
AI.motivation: When minority observations are fewer than features, maximum likelihood suffers from quasi-complete separation, penalized likelihood shows severe intercept bias, and SMOTE collapses into an (n1 - 1)-dimensional affine subspace.
AI.method: The paradigm shifts from minority interpolation to majority fringe extrapolation. Stein's Lemma shows that the majority conditional-expectation shift induced by logistic truncation identifies the hyperplane normal after Mahalanobis whitening, and synthetic minority points are extrapolated from the high-quantile majority fringe along the conjugate direction. A hybrid estimator adds majority third-moment skewness and a location-shift-invariant zero-boundary intercept calibration for semi-supervised and supervised settings.
AI.result: Monte Carlo simulations and real benchmarks (Wisconsin Diagnostic Breast Cancer and Banknote Authentication) with n1 of 3 or 5 show that the approach prevents parameter divergence, recovers the oracle hyperplane with high fidelity, and substantially outperforms Firth's regression and SMOTE in F1-score and estimation stability.
AI.conclusion: Majority-fringe extrapolation with the proposed intercept calibration offers a stable route to estimation and classification under extreme rarity with rank-deficient minority data.

title: Pair-Dependent Judge Errors Change the Minimax Rate of Semantic Entropy
comment: 47 pages, 5 figures, 3 tables. Code: this https URL
summary: Semantic entropy, the entropy of the meanings among a language model's sampled answers, is estimated from the verdicts of a judge that declares pairs of answers equivalent or not, and automatic judges err in ways that depend on the answers they compare. The existing minimax theory covers only judges whose false-equivalence probability is the same for all pairs. We model a known judge that declares two answers with meanings $a$ and $b$ equivalent with probability $q+\Delta M_{ab}$, for a symmetric matrix $M$ and $q$ bounded away from $0$ and $1$, and show that for three meanings the rate is set by tree statistics on four answers, while on an open set of channels the consistency threshold is set by trees on five. For every channel in an explicit open class, the minimax squared risk is of order $N^{-1/3}$ with $N=n^4\Delta^6$ on polynomial weak windows on which $n^5\Delta^8$ exceeds a multiple of $\log n$, and of order $\min\{1,N^{-1/3}\}$ on every polynomial weak window when the tree functions on at most four vertices are injective. The exponent comes from a cubic degeneracy at the equitable point. On an open set of channels in the class, the four-vertex tree functions take equal values at two distributions with different entropies. For such a channel, on every polynomial weak window, the minimax risk is of the order of the sum of $\min\{1,N^{-1/3}\}$ and a term that decays exponentially in $n^5\Delta^8$, so no estimator is consistent while $n^5\Delta^8$ stays bounded, even as $N\to\infty$. For $\Delta=n^{-\beta}$ with $\beta>1/2$, channels of the class with injective four-vertex tree functions allow consistent estimation exactly for $\beta<2/3$, and the channels of this open set exactly for $\beta<5/8$, at which the risk exponent drops from $1/12$ to $0$. Computer-assisted certificates show that both kinds of channels occur on open sets.

AI.tldr: The paper models a judge whose equivalence errors depend on the pair of answers being compared and shows that this changes the minimax rate of semantic entropy estimation. Depending on the channel, the squared risk ranges from order N^(-1/3) to a regime where no estimator is consistent while n^5 Delta^8 stays bounded.
AI.motivation: Semantic entropy is estimated from a judge's equivalence verdicts, but the existing minimax theory covers only judges whose false-equivalence probability is the same for all pairs, while automatic judges err in answer-dependent ways.
AI.method: A known judge declares answers with meanings a and b equivalent with probability q + Delta M_ab, where M is a symmetric matrix and q is bounded away from 0 and 1. The analysis uses tree statistics on four answers for three meanings and on five answers for an open set of channels, supported by computer-assisted certificates.
AI.result: For every channel in an explicit open class, the minimax squared risk is of order N^(-1/3) with N = n^4 Delta^6 on polynomial weak windows. On an open set of channels, four-vertex tree functions take equal values at two distributions with different entropies, so the minimax risk is the sum of min(1, N^(-1/3)) and a term decaying exponentially in n^5 Delta^8, and no estimator is consistent while n^5 Delta^8 stays bounded. For Delta = n^(-beta) with beta > 1/2, consistency holds exactly for beta < 2/3 for injective-tree channels and for beta < 5/8 for the open-set channels, where the risk exponent drops from 1/12 to 0.
AI.conclusion: Answer-dependent judge errors change both the achievable rate and the consistency thresholds for semantic entropy, so the judge's error structure must be modeled rather than assumed uniform.

title: Event2Reward: Learning Robotic Rewards from Progress Relations
summary: Learning task progress from robot demonstrations provides a practical way to construct dense shaping rewards for robotic reinforcement learning. A common approach uses normalized demonstration time as progress labels, implicitly assuming monotonically increasing task progress. During policy exploration, however, actual task progress can stall or even regress. Such models may mistake regressions for progress, assigning positive shaping rewards to actions that cause progress loss. Real suboptimal and failed executions offer corrective experience, but assigning absolute progress values to their states is difficult. Our key observation is that stalls, regressions, and recoveries establish local relative progress relations even when absolute progress is unknown. We introduce Event2Reward, which uses normalized temporal labels to anchor the progress scale and these within-trajectory relations to constrain local changes, combining absolute and relative progress supervision. Its progress predictions serve as potentials for reward shaping. We curate an event-annotated dataset from approximately 100K raw real-robot execution records, covering successful, suboptimal, and failed executions, without requiring framewise absolute progress labels. Under the same training budgets, Event2Reward improves average policy success by 18.16 percentage points over a baseline using only sparse task rewards across 40 tasks in four LIBERO suites. On real robots, average success after 30 minutes of wall-clock training reaches 60.0% on three precise insertion tasks and 90.0% on three object manipulation tasks, exceeding the sparse-reward baseline under the same budget by 36.7 and 23.3 percentage points, respectively. Ablation studies further show that absolute progress supervision and relative progress relations are complementary, with joint supervision yielding better downstream policy learning.

AI.tldr: Event2Reward learns robot task-progress potentials from normalized temporal labels plus within-trajectory relative progress relations, and uses them for reward shaping. It improves average policy success over sparse-reward training across 40 LIBERO tasks and on real robots.
AI.motivation: Demonstration-time progress labels assume monotonic progress, so stalls and regressions are mistaken for progress and actions that lose progress receive positive shaping rewards, while absolute progress values for failed executions are hard to assign.
AI.method: Normalized temporal labels anchor the progress scale, and relations within each trajectory, arising from stalls, regressions, and recoveries, constrain local changes, combining absolute and relative supervision. The progress predictions serve as potentials for reward shaping. An event-annotated dataset is curated from about 100K raw real-robot records covering successful, suboptimal, and failed executions.
AI.result: Under the same training budgets, Event2Reward improves average policy success by 18.16 percentage points over a sparse-reward baseline across 40 tasks in four LIBERO suites. On real robots after 30 minutes of wall-clock training, success reaches 60.0% on three precise insertion tasks and 90.0% on three object manipulation tasks, exceeding the sparse baseline by 36.7 and 23.3 percentage points. Ablations show that absolute and relative progress supervision are complementary.
AI.conclusion: Relative progress relations recovered from failed and suboptimal executions complement absolute progress supervision, and joint supervision yields better downstream policy learning.

title: Unlocking Any-Order Generation in Pretrained Autoregressive Image Models
comment: Accepted in NeurIPS 2026, Sydney as a poster
summary: Autoregressive (AR) image generators are powerful in principle but inflexible in practice: training with a fixed raster-scan order hardcodes a single factorization of the image distribution into the model, leaving it unable to inpaint, outpaint, or edit at inference time. Existing solutions, including the modern discrete-diffusion family, train from scratch on a mixture of token orderings, paying roughly 3x the compute of standard raster-scan training; discrete diffusion further sacrifices compatibility with the AR inference ecosystem (KV caching, vLLM) by construction. We argue that this cost is unnecessary. A pretrained raster-scan AR model has already learned the joint distribution over image tokens; what it lacks is not knowledge but the ability to express that knowledge through non-sequential conditional pathways. We propose a recipe for adapting pretrained raster-scan models into any-order generators using two components: future-aware positional embeddings that resolve a target-position identifiability problem at negligible overhead, and an ordering curriculum that traces a stable optimization path from the pretrained solution to a good any-order basin. Applied to four base models across two architectures and two scales (LlamaGen-L/XL, RAR-L/XL), the recipe substantially outperforms MaskGIT on ImageNet inpainting (FID 6.21 vs. 10.44) and outpainting, is competitive with MAR-L, trades a 1.2-1.9 increase in class-conditional FID for this flexibility, and costs 13-33% additional compute beyond pretraining, while leaving the standard AR inference stack untouched. Inpainting, outpainting, and editing, our results suggest, need not be added to autoregressive image models. They can be unlocked from the ones that exist. Code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: The paper adapts pretrained raster-scan autoregressive image models into any-order generators using future-aware positional embeddings and an ordering curriculum, which enables inpainting, outpainting, and editing. The adaptation adds 13-33% compute beyond pretraining and leaves the standard AR inference stack untouched.
AI.motivation: Raster-scan AR image models cannot inpaint, outpaint, or edit at inference time, and existing any-order solutions such as discrete diffusion train from scratch at roughly 3x the compute of raster training and lose compatibility with AR inference such as KV caching.
AI.method: Two components are used: future-aware positional embeddings that resolve a target-position identifiability problem at negligible overhead, and an ordering curriculum that traces a stable optimization path from the pretrained solution to a good any-order basin. The recipe is applied to LlamaGen-L/XL and RAR-L/XL.
AI.result: On ImageNet inpainting the recipe substantially outperforms MaskGIT (FID 6.21 vs. 10.44), and it also substantially outperforms MaskGIT on outpainting and is competitive with MAR-L. The flexibility costs a 1.2-1.9 increase in class-conditional FID.
AI.conclusion: Inpainting, outpainting, and editing can be unlocked from existing pretrained autoregressive image models at modest extra cost, without training from scratch or changing the AR inference stack.

title: BEVLight: Generalizable Traffic Signal Control from UAV Bird's-Eye Views
summary: Learning-based traffic signal control (TSC) has achieved promising performance, but most methods rely on structured traffic states that must be estimated from sensor observations in real deployments. Visual TSC learns signal decisions directly from images, yet existing methods depend on fixed roadside cameras and remain tied to specific intersection configurations and visual domains. UAVs offer on-demand bird's-eye-view (BEV) observations that jointly capture intersection topology and traffic dynamics, making them a promising sensing platform for visual TSC. We present BEVLight, a generalizable TSC framework that directly maps BEV observations to signal actions. BEVLight grounds visual features onto individual lanes and composes them along the junction topology into movement and phase representations, allowing a shared policy to score candidate phases across heterogeneous intersection layouts and signal plans. To train the policy, we develop a web-based virtual teleoperation platform and collect over 5K human control decisions together with their underlying traffic states. Simulator-provided traffic states first supervise lane- and movement-level representations, after which human phase selections and rankings supervise the phase scorer. Re-rendering the recorded trajectories under diverse appearances preserves both forms of supervision and encourages robustness to visual changes. Closed-loop experiments demonstrate zero-shot generalization across traffic demands, signal plans, and intersections: BEVLight reduces average waiting time by 7--9\% relative to perception-to-control visual baselines and matches or outperforms structured-state RL controllers that receive ground-truth traffic states, achieving the lowest waiting time in 12 of 16 scenarios. An offline study further shows that BEVLight transfers to real UAV observations without target-domain adaptation.

AI.tldr: BEVLight is a generalizable traffic signal control framework that maps UAV bird's-eye-view observations directly to signal actions by grounding visual features onto lanes and composing them into movement and phase representations. It cuts waiting time relative to visual baselines, matches or beats RL controllers given ground-truth states, and generalizes zero-shot across intersections.
AI.motivation: Structured-state controllers need traffic states estimated from sensors, while existing visual controllers rely on fixed roadside cameras tied to specific intersection configurations and visual domains, whereas UAVs offer on-demand bird's-eye views.
AI.method: Visual features are grounded onto individual lanes and composed along the junction topology into movement and phase representations, and a shared policy scores candidate phases. Training uses over 5K human control decisions collected on a web-based virtual teleoperation platform, with simulator traffic states supervising lane and movement representations and human phase selections and rankings supervising the phase scorer. Recorded trajectories are re-rendered under diverse appearances.
AI.result: Closed-loop experiments show zero-shot generalization across traffic demands, signal plans, and intersections. BEVLight reduces average waiting time by 7-9% relative to perception-to-control visual baselines, matches or outperforms RL controllers that receive ground-truth states, and achieves the lowest waiting time in 12 of 16 scenarios. An offline study shows transfer to real UAV observations without target-domain adaptation.
AI.conclusion: Lane-grounded bird's-eye-view representations trained with simulator and human supervision enable a generalizable UAV-based visual traffic signal controller that transfers to real observations.

title: Satisficing Regret Minimization in Bandits with Knapsacks
summary: We study satisficing regret minimization in bandits with knapsacks (BwK), where a learner sequentially selects randomized policies, i.e., distributions over arms, to obtain mean rewards above a satisficing threshold as frequently as possible while respecting finite resource budgets. The performance is measured by satisficing regret, the cumulative deficits of the selected policies' mean rewards below this threshold. Resource constraints introduce two difficulties: an algorithm can incur linear satisficing regret even with small standard regret as deficits to the threshold cannot be compensated, and random consumption can cause early resource depletion even when policies are feasible in expectation. To address these challenges, we propose SELECTwK, a general algorithmic template that uses a BwK learning oracle algorithm with sub-linear expected (standard) regret upper bound to search for and test candidate satisficing policies (i.e., policies whose mean rewards exceed satisficing threshold and whose expected resource consumption is feasible over the time horizon). Our regret analysis, supported by an LP-duality argument, establishes that SELECTwK attains constant expected satisficing regret when a satisficing policy exists. We further introduce a stronger regret condition that bounds the expected sum of positive reward deficits to the optimal one at each time step, under which SELECTwK achieves a sharper constant bound together with a sub-linear bound in the time horizon. As a complement, SELECTwK still preserves the oracle's sub-linear expected standard regret bound if the satisficing threshold is unattainable. Finally, we establish the oracle conditions and corresponding satisficing regret bound for existing finite-armed BwK and dynamic pricing algorithms, and conduct numerical experiments on dynamic pricing with limited inventory to demonstrate the empirical performance of SELECTwK.

AI.tldr: SELECTwK is an algorithmic template for satisficing regret in bandits with knapsacks: it searches for feasible policies whose mean rewards exceed a threshold and attains constant expected satisficing regret when such a policy exists. It keeps sub-linear standard regret when the threshold is unattainable.
AI.motivation: Under resource constraints, satisficing regret can grow linearly even when standard regret is small, because deficits below the threshold cannot be compensated, and random consumption can deplete resources early even when policies are feasible in expectation.
AI.method: The learner selects randomized policies. SELECTwK uses a BwK learning oracle with sub-linear expected regret to search for and test candidate satisficing policies, meaning policies whose mean rewards exceed the threshold and whose expected resource consumption is feasible over the horizon. The regret analysis is supported by an LP-duality argument.
AI.result: SELECTwK attains constant expected satisficing regret when a satisficing policy exists. Under a stronger condition bounding expected positive reward deficits, it achieves a sharper constant together with a sub-linear horizon bound. If the threshold is unattainable, it still preserves the oracle's sub-linear expected standard regret. Existing finite-armed BwK and dynamic pricing algorithms are shown to satisfy the oracle conditions, and numerical experiments on dynamic pricing with limited inventory demonstrate performance.
AI.conclusion: Satisficing regret under resource constraints can be controlled by an oracle-based search template, which gives constant regret whenever a feasible satisficing policy exists.

title: Semantic Mismapping in Generalized Category Discovery: Evaluation and Mitigation
summary: Generalized Category Discovery (GCD) aims to perform old-category recognition and novel-category discovery in the same unlabeled set. Early methods address both objectives through clustering and evaluate the exchangeable predicted indices with global Hungarian (GH) matching. Recent methods adopt trainable parametric heads, using supervision for old-category recognition and discovery-oriented objectives for new categories. In this way, the output space becomes partially exchangeable: old indices are semantically anchored, while new indices remain exchangeable. However, these methods still apply global matching, which can reassign anchored old indices to other categories and hide some prediction errors. Empirically, we are surprised to observe that this reassignment can induce an overestimation of new-category accuracy by up to 25.63 points. We term this phenomenon semantic mismapping and further derive a permutation-cycle condition that characterizes when semantic mismapping can increase the global matching score. To fix this issue, we propose Semantics-Preserving Evaluation (SPE), which preserves the supervised semantics of old indices and restricts Hungarian matching to the new region. Furthermore, we propose Mismapping-Mitigating Optimization (MMO) to alleviate the prediction errors that can give rise to semantic mismapping, combining a region-balance loss (RBL) for old/new routing with a novel-diversity loss (NDL) that encourages orthogonality among new prototypes. Theoretically, we show that minimizing the two losses can tighten an upper bound on spurious accuracy gains from semantic mismapping, with controllable residual terms. Empirical results under both GH and SPE demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed method.

AI.tldr: The paper identifies semantic mismapping in generalized category discovery, where global Hungarian matching reassigns semantically anchored old-category indices and can overestimate new-category accuracy by up to 25.63 points. It proposes Semantics-Preserving Evaluation and Mismapping-Mitigating Optimization to counter this effect.
AI.motivation: Recent methods use trainable heads whose old indices are semantically anchored while new indices remain exchangeable, but they still apply global matching, which can reassign anchored old indices and hide some prediction errors.
AI.method: A permutation-cycle condition characterizes when semantic mismapping can increase the global matching score. Semantics-Preserving Evaluation (SPE) preserves the supervised semantics of old indices and restricts Hungarian matching to the new region. Mismapping-Mitigating Optimization (MMO) combines a region-balance loss for old/new routing with a novel-diversity loss that encourages orthogonality among new prototypes.
AI.result: Global matching can overestimate new-category accuracy by up to 25.63 points. Empirical results under both global Hungarian matching and SPE demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method. Theoretically, minimizing the two losses can tighten an upper bound on spurious accuracy gains from semantic mismapping, with controllable residual terms.
AI.conclusion: Evaluation must preserve the supervised semantics of old-category indices, and the proposed losses reduce the spurious accuracy gains that mismapping introduces.

title: FDSML: Formula-Driven Supervised Metric Learning with Parameter-Aware Triplet Loss
comment: Accepted to WACV 2027. 24 pages (11 main + 13 supplementary). Project page: this https URL
summary: Formula-Driven Supervised Learning (FDSL) enables vision pre-training without real images, but existing methods cast pre-training as classification on discretized labels, discarding continuity in the generative process. We propose Formula-Driven Supervised Metric Learning (FDSML), which derives relational supervision from image-generation parameters beyond discrete class labels. FDSML combines FineFractalDB, our refined fractal dataset with higher intra-class variation and more stable structures, with a Parameter-Aware Triplet (PA-Triplet) Loss that assigns positives and negatives according to distances in the underlying Iterated Function System parameter space. This objective trains embeddings to respect parameter-derived relative similarity orderings. Experiments show that FDSML improves transferability to image retrieval while remaining competitive on downstream classification and improving robustness under several corruption settings. On ResNet-50, Recall@1 improves from 65.6% to 74.0% on Stanford Online Products and from 56.2% to 78.4% on Stanford Cars over FDSL pre-training. These results suggest that parameter-derived relational supervision provides a stronger synthetic pre-training signal than label-based classification for transfer beyond recognition.

AI.tldr: FDSML improves formula-driven pretraining by learning from the generation parameters of an Iterated Function System rather than discrete class labels, using a refined fractal dataset and a parameter-aware triplet loss. It improves transfer to image retrieval, for example Recall@1 on Stanford Cars rises from 56.2% to 78.4% with ResNet-50.
AI.motivation: Formula-driven supervised learning pretrains without real images, but it casts pretraining as classification on discretized labels, which discards the continuity of the generative process.
AI.method: FineFractalDB, a refined fractal dataset with higher intra-class variation and more stable structures, is combined with a Parameter-Aware Triplet (PA-Triplet) loss that assigns positives and negatives according to distances in the underlying Iterated Function System parameter space, so that embeddings respect parameter-derived similarity orderings.
AI.result: On ResNet-50, Recall@1 improves from 65.6% to 74.0% on Stanford Online Products and from 56.2% to 78.4% on Stanford Cars over FDSL pretraining. The method remains competitive on downstream classification and improves robustness under several corruption settings.
AI.conclusion: Parameter-derived relational supervision gives a stronger synthetic pretraining signal than label-based classification for transfer beyond recognition, such as retrieval.

title: Does Federated Training Degrade Explainability? A Comparative Analysis of Grad-CAM Faithfulness in Centralized vs. Federated Deepfake Detection
comment: 10 Pages, 3 figures, Muhammad Uzair Shahid and Muhammad Zabil Mehboob contributed equally to this work
summary: Automated detection has become the essential safeguard against realistic synthetic media, but deploying it at scale requires training on sensitive data from multiple organizations, putting privacy and the transparency demanded by forensic review in direct conflict. Federated learning resolves the privacy side by sharing only model updates rather than raw data, but whether this comes at the cost of trustworthy gradient-based explanations, which analysts rely on to decide whether or not to trust a flagged clip, has not been studied. We present the systematic study of Grad-CAM explanation faithfulness under federated deepfake detection, evaluating an EfficientNet-B4 detector on FaceForensics++ across five federated clients under varying degrees of data heterogeneity. We find that the relationship between federation and explanation quality is non-monotonic: at near-IID (Independent and Identically Distributed Data) and moderate heterogeneity, federated models match or exceed the faithfulness of a centralized baseline, but at extreme heterogeneity, explanations break down entirely, becoming spatially incoherent and, on average, causally misleading. This degradation is not a general cost of federated training but a threshold effect tied to client heterogeneity, and we offer practical guidance for identifying when privacy-preserving deepfake detection can be deployed safely and when its explanations can no longer be trusted. Code and data partitions are available for reproducibility.

AI.tldr: The paper studies whether federated training of an EfficientNet-B4 deepfake detector degrades the faithfulness of Grad-CAM explanations relative to centralized training. Federated models match or exceed centralized faithfulness at near-IID and moderate heterogeneity, but the explanations break down at extreme heterogeneity.
AI.motivation: Deepfake detection at scale requires training on sensitive data from multiple organizations, and federated learning addresses privacy, but whether it compromises the gradient-based explanations that analysts rely on had not been studied.
AI.method: A systematic evaluation of Grad-CAM faithfulness for an EfficientNet-B4 detector on FaceForensics++, with five federated clients under varying degrees of data heterogeneity, compared against a centralized baseline.
AI.result: The relationship between federation and explanation quality is non-monotonic. At near-IID and moderate heterogeneity, federated models match or exceed the faithfulness of the centralized baseline, whereas at extreme heterogeneity the explanations become spatially incoherent and, on average, causally misleading.
AI.conclusion: The degradation is a threshold effect tied to client heterogeneity rather than a general cost of federated training, and the work gives guidance on when privacy-preserving deepfake detection can be deployed with trustworthy explanations.

title: Distilling Large-Scale Machine Learning Interatomic Potentials to Predict Long-Timescale Electrolyte Transport Properties
summary: Accurately predicting the transport properties of liquid electrolytes is critical for next-generation battery design and requires force fields that are both quantum-mechanically accurate and fast enough for long-timescale simulation. Recent large-scale pretrained machine learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) approach density-functional-theory accuracy, but remain too slow to access the necessary timescales to converge transport properties. We provide a knowledge distillation procedure to transfer the accuracy of a large-scale "teacher" MLIP into fast, system-specific "students", without any additional ab initio data. Our distilled models run ~40x faster, reproduce teacher-predicted structural observables, and produce stable 20 ns trajectories in days, rather than the months the teacher would require. Across a diverse set of sodium- and lithium-ion electrolytes, student-predicted self-diffusivities, ionic conductivities, and shear viscosities track experiment and outperform classical force-field predictions, establishing distillation as a practical route to accurate, long-timescale simulations necessary for high-throughput electrolyte screening.

AI.tldr: The paper distills a large pretrained machine learning interatomic potential into fast, system-specific student models that run about 40 times faster and produce stable 20 ns trajectories in days. Student-predicted transport properties track experiment for sodium- and lithium-ion electrolytes and outperform classical force fields.
AI.motivation: Predicting transport properties of liquid electrolytes requires quantum-mechanically accurate force fields that are fast enough for long timescales, but large pretrained machine learning interatomic potentials are still too slow to converge transport properties.
AI.method: A knowledge distillation procedure transfers the accuracy of a large-scale teacher MLIP into fast, system-specific student models, without any additional ab initio data.
AI.result: The distilled models run about 40x faster, reproduce the teacher's predicted structural observables, and produce stable 20 ns trajectories in days rather than the months the teacher would require. Across diverse sodium- and lithium-ion electrolytes, student-predicted self-diffusivities, ionic conductivities, and shear viscosities track experiment and outperform classical force-field predictions.
AI.conclusion: Distillation is a practical route to accurate, long-timescale simulation for high-throughput electrolyte screening.

title: Conic-Lifting for Learning-rate-free Convex Optimization
summary: A central topic in online and stochastic optimization is to design algorithms that do not require tuning of hyperparameters. Successful strategies in online learning include AdaGrad-style learning rates, Conic Blackwell algorithms, and parameter-free algorithms. However, these classes require different, often difficult, analyses. We develop a unifying family of Online Convex Optimization (OCO) algorithms that require no user-tuned learning rate on convex domains that may be unbounded. The construction lifts the domain to a cone by adding one scalar coordinate, an idea going back to Blackwell (1954). The lifted subgradients are orthogonal to the corresponding lifted decisions, leaving the comparator scale free to optimize in the regret analysis. Applying Follow-the-Regularized-Leader (FTRL) and Online Mirror Descent (OMD) on the cone recovers Conic Blackwell Algorithm (CBA) and Conic Blackwell Algorithm Plus (CBA$^+$) on bounded domains in Hilbert spaces and extends them to finite-dimensional normed spaces with a strongly convex squared norm. For arbitrary nonempty closed convex domains in these spaces, a known gradient bound yields parameter-free regret guarantees. Surprisingly, on an unconstrained Hilbert space, the construction recovers the Krichevsky--Trofimov (KT) coin-betting algorithm exactly. We also give a parameter-free algorithm for unconstrained domains that requires no gradient bound.

AI.tldr: The paper builds a unifying family of online convex optimization algorithms that need no tuned learning rate, by lifting the domain to a cone with one extra scalar coordinate. It recovers Conic Blackwell algorithms and the KT coin-betting algorithm and gives parameter-free regret guarantees for unbounded convex domains.
AI.motivation: Existing learning-rate-free strategies (AdaGrad-style learning rates, Conic Blackwell algorithms, parameter-free algorithms) each require different and often difficult analyses.
AI.method: The convex domain is lifted to a cone by adding one scalar coordinate, an idea going back to Blackwell (1954), so that lifted subgradients are orthogonal to lifted decisions. Follow-the-Regularized-Leader and Online Mirror Descent are then run on the cone.
AI.result: On bounded domains in Hilbert spaces the construction recovers CBA and CBA+, and it extends them to finite-dimensional normed spaces with a strongly convex squared norm. For arbitrary closed convex domains a known gradient bound yields parameter-free regret guarantees. On unconstrained Hilbert space it recovers the KT coin-betting algorithm exactly, and a parameter-free algorithm for unconstrained domains is given that needs no gradient bound.
AI.conclusion: A single construction unifies several parameter-free online learning strategies that previously required separate analyses, and it also covers the case where no gradient bound is available.

title: ROAD: Modern Adversarial Training for Simple One-Step Distillation at Scale
summary: One-step distillation turns pretrained diffusion models into fast generators, but strong results often require substantial training machinery and compute. Pure adversarial distillation offers a simpler route, yet has struggled at modern text-to-image scale. To address this limitation, we propose ROAD (Representation-grounded One-step Adversarial Distillation), a one-stage framework that distills text-to-image models with one adversarial objective and a lightweight representation-space critic. First, we replace the classical convolutional head with a Lipschitz-controlled Transformer head with token-level text conditioning, which matches the semantic tokens of modern visual encoders. Second, we observed a fixed random feature mixing leads to long-horizon degradation. We attribute it to generator-critic co-adaptation around one realization-specific view, and periodically re-draw the mixing to keep the randomization effective. Third, for our dense and vector-valued logits, we introduce Jacobian R1 which penalizes the full input-logit Jacobian, overcoming pooled R1's limitation of neglecting most of logit sensitivities. A single adversarial objective then suffices: in one step, ROAD reaches 11.03 FID on SDXL and 13.73 on SD3.5-M on COCO-10K, surpassing the multi-step teachers at a fraction of distribution matching's training compute.

AI.tldr: ROAD is a one-stage adversarial distillation framework that turns text-to-image diffusion models into one-step generators using one adversarial objective and a lightweight representation-space critic. It reaches 11.03 FID on SDXL and 13.73 on SD3.5-M on COCO-10K in one step, surpassing the multi-step teachers.
AI.motivation: One-step distillation of diffusion models often needs heavy training machinery and compute, while pure adversarial distillation has struggled at modern text-to-image scale.
AI.method: Three components: a Lipschitz-controlled Transformer head with token-level text conditioning in place of the classical convolutional head; periodic re-drawing of a fixed random feature mixing to avoid long-horizon degradation caused by generator-critic co-adaptation; and Jacobian R1, which penalizes the full input-logit Jacobian rather than pooled R1.
AI.result: In one step ROAD reaches 11.03 FID on SDXL and 13.73 on SD3.5-M on COCO-10K, surpassing the multi-step teachers at a fraction of distribution matching's training compute.
AI.conclusion: A single adversarial objective suffices for competitive one-step text-to-image distillation at modern scale, at much lower training cost than distribution matching.

title: The Cost of Working Memory in Streaming Mean Estimation
summary: A streaming estimator must compute from the evidence that fits in memory. We determine when storing an accurate mean is easier than computing it. For Gaussian mean estimation over the Euclidean unit ball in $\mathbb{R}^d$, we establish the minimax rate under squared error with $K$ persistent states, a known horizon, and a public time index: $\min\{1, K^{-2/d}+\frac{d}{n} (1+\frac{\log(ed)}{1+(\log K)/d})\}$. Unrestricted computation followed by $K$-level encoding has rate $\min\{1,d/n+K^{-2/d}\}$. At a fixed sufficiently small error, statistically optimal sample size therefore requires order $d\log d$ working bits, while order $d$ bits suffice to store the answer. The lower bound tracks repeated state compression through an entropy potential obtained by Gaussian smoothing. A matching construction combines a multiscale modular counter with workspace reused across coordinate groups. In one dimension, it attains the terminal rate $n^{-1}+K^{-2}$. Any fixed confidence requirement that the realized loss not exceed the zero baseline preserves these rates. Increasing confidence creates a further memory requirement: at fixed nontrivial risk in every fixed dimension, failure probability $e^{-\gamma n}$ requires and permits order $\log n$ working states for sufficiently small fixed $\gamma>0$.
